title: Practice Test 4: Claude Certified Architect - Foundations
description:
60 scenario-based questions drawn from 4 of 6 official scenarios. Questions follow the exam guide's domain weightings: Agentic Architecture (27%), Tool Design & MCP (18%), Claude Code (20%), Prompt Engineering (20%), and Context Management (15%).

As with the real exam, every question is based on one of four specific scenarios selected at random for the exam. You'll find the same general scenarios repeated throughout the questions, with specific challenges aligned with the tasks and domains of the exam guide.

Each question presents a realistic production situation with one correct answer and three plausible distractors, including common anti-patterns. Detailed explanations with documentation links follow each answer.

Prerequisite: Review the official exam guide and complete Anthropic's free certification preparation courses (or have equivalent hands-on experience).

prompt.question:
SCENARIO: You are integrating Claude Code into your Continuous Integration/Continuous Deployment (CI/CD) pipeline. The system runs automated code reviews, generates test cases, and provides feedback on pull requests. You need to design prompts that provide actionable feedback and minimize false positives.

QUESTION: A developer must rebuild the pipeline's test-generation harness, a change touching more than 40 files with several viable integration strategies and unclear dependencies. How should the developer begin this work in Claude Code?
answers: Start in direct execution and switch to plan mode only when the work becomes complicated.
Start in plan mode to explore the codebase and approve a plan before edits begin.
Execute immediately and run /compact regularly so the growing context never derails the work.
Begin direct execution with detailed upfront instructions that specify every file change in advance.
feedbacks: With this approach, Claude makes edits under a strategy that nobody has chosen yet, before any planning starts. This can lead to costly rework. The size and ambiguity of the change are known from the start, so planning should come first, not after problems appear.

Plan mode is designed for this situation: large changes, several possible approaches, and unclear dependencies. Claude explores the codebase without editing files and presents a plan for review. A wrong approach is caught before any code changes, so expensive rework is avoided.

The /compact command reduces pressure on the context window by summarizing the conversation history. It does nothing to decide which of several integration strategies is correct. Compressing the context cannot replace exploring the codebase and choosing a design before editing.

Writing complete instructions in advance assumes that the developer already understands the dependencies and has chosen the right strategy. The scenario says this is not the case. Plan mode exists so that this understanding is built through safe exploration before any edits are made.
prompt.explanation:
Plan mode is one of Claude Code's permission modes. While it is active, Claude can read files and explore the codebase, but it does not edit source files. Instead, it produces an implementation plan that the developer reviews and approves. Only after approval does the session switch modes and start making changes. The key idea is design before commitment. For a change that touches 40+ files and has several possible integration strategies, it is much cheaper to revise a written plan than to revise partly finished edits spread across the codebase.

The choice depends on scope and ambiguity. Direct execution suits well-understood, narrowly scoped changes, such as a single-file fix with a clear stack trace. Plan mode suits work with architectural impact, many files, competing approaches, or unfamiliar dependencies. Starting in direct execution and switching to planning only when trouble appears reverses this order. By the time the complexity becomes visible, edits based on a strategy that nobody reviewed already exist and may need to be undone. In the same way, specifying every change in advance assumes knowledge that the exploration phase is meant to produce. And /compact solves a different problem: context window pressure in long sessions, not the choice of strategy.

A common workflow combines both modes. Plan first, review the plan carefully instead of reading it quickly, approve it, and then carry out the agreed approach. You can enter plan mode with Shift+Tab, with the /plan command, or by starting the CLI with --permission-mode plan. See Permission modes for how plan mode blocks edits and how approving the plan moves the session into implementation.

QUESTION: To cut API costs, this team moved both its nightly test generation and its blocking pull request review step to the Message Batches API. Developers now sometimes wait hours for review feedback before they can merge. What should the team change?
answers: Move both workflows back to synchronous calls to keep one consistent API pattern.
Poll the batch status more frequently so review results are retrieved the moment processing finishes.
Return the pull request review step to synchronous calls and keep nightly test generation on batches.
Submit each pull request review as its own single-request batch so smaller batches complete sooner.
feedbacks: Moving both workflows back to synchronous calls would fix the review delay. But it gives up the 50% batch savings on nightly test generation for no reason. Nightly test generation is a non-blocking workload that can accept delays, which is the kind of workload the discount is designed for. Each workload should use the API that fits its latency requirement. It should not be forced into one pattern.

Polling more often only shortens the gap between when the batch finishes and when you retrieve the results. It does not change the processing time. The Message Batches API has no latency guarantee and can take up to 24 hours, so a blocking check can still delay merges for hours.

Pull request review is a blocking workflow: developers wait for the results. So it needs the immediate responses of the synchronous API. Nightly test generation can accept delays and does not block anyone, so it is still a good fit for the batch discount.

Batch size does not create a latency guarantee. Even a batch with one request is processed asynchronously, with no SLA, and may take up to 24 hours. A blocking workflow cannot depend on that time window, no matter how the batch is split.
prompt.explanation:
The Message Batches API gives lower cost in exchange for higher latency. Requests are processed asynchronously at a 50% discount. Results are available only when the batch completes, and there is no guaranteed turnaround within the processing window of up to 24 hours. Anthropic states that most batches finish in under an hour. That is an observation, not an SLA, so no workload that a person is actively waiting on should depend on it. The rule is to match each workload to its latency requirement. Blocking workflows, such as a pull request review that must pass before a merge, stay on the synchronous Messages API. Non-blocking workloads that can accept delays, such as nightly test generation or weekly audits, go to batches and get the savings.

The incorrect approaches either try to make an asynchronous mechanism behave like a synchronous one, or they correct too much. Polling more often only reduces the delay between batch completion and result retrieval. It cannot speed up processing. Reducing a batch to a single request does not change the asynchronous model or add a latency guarantee. Moving both workflows back to synchronous calls would fix the review delay, but it gives up the discount on the workload that fits the batch model best.

The key idea is a table with two columns. One column is for blocking, interactive work (synchronous API). The other is for scheduled, bulk, or deferred work (batch API). See Batch processing for the suitability criteria, the 24-hour window, and polling behavior.

QUESTION: The pipeline extracts acceptance criteria from design documents in pull requests. Some documents state criteria inline in narrative prose; others use structured requirements tables. Despite detailed instructions covering both formats, extraction remains inconsistent. What change most reliably improves consistency?
answers: Add a few-shot example of correct extraction from each document structure, with brief reasoning.
Run the extraction three times per document and keep the output produced by the majority.
Require teams to rewrite design documents into one standard template before extraction runs.
Expand the instructions with more detailed written rules describing each document structure explicitly.
feedbacks: Few-shot examples are the documented technique for making output consistent when detailed instructions alone do not work. One targeted example for each document structure shows the model how to find and extract criteria from ordinary sentences and from tables. Written rules have difficulty explaining this kind of judgment.

Majority voting reduces random differences between runs. But it does not teach the model how to extract criteria from narrative prose (ordinary sentences, not structured data). If the model misreads a structure in the same way every time, the majority output will be wrong every time.

Forcing document authors to use one template moves the work onto the developers instead of improving the extraction system. The model can handle different structures reliably once examples show the correct handling of each one.

Detailed instructions that describe both formats are already in place, and they have not produced consistent results. Adding more written rules repeats a technique that has already failed in this scenario. Examples, in contrast, show the expected extraction concretely.
prompt.explanation:
Sometimes a model must do the same task on source documents with different structures. In this case, the problem is rarely that the model cannot read one of the structures. The problem is that written instructions cannot fully explain what the extraction should look like in each case. Few-shot examples fix this by showing the judgment directly. One example shows criteria taken from narrative prose (ordinary sentences, not structured data), and one shows criteria taken from a structured table. Together they give the model a concrete pattern to generalize from. This is why Anthropic describes multishot prompting as one of the most reliable ways to control output format and consistency. The examples should be relevant to the real documents. They should be varied enough to cover the structures that actually appear. They should also be clearly separated from the real input, so the model can tell examples from live input.

Instructions state rules, while examples show decisions. A rule like "criteria may appear in prose or in tables" tells the model that variation exists. An example shows what a correct extraction from each variant looks like, including which surrounding text to ignore. That is why adding more written rules is tempting but weaker. That approach has already failed in this scenario. Majority voting over repeated runs only averages out randomness. It cannot correct a systematic misreading of one document structure. Requiring a single documentation template makes every author do extra work to make up for a prompt weakness that the pipeline can fix itself.

In practice, two to four targeted examples are usually enough, each with brief reasoning about why that extraction is correct. The goal is to cover the structures that are really ambiguous, not to add many examples. See Claude prompting best practices and Increase output consistency for guidance on structuring and separating examples.

QUESTION: The reviewer currently posts every finding as a blocking pull request comment, and developers complain that uncertain findings waste their time. The team wants confident findings posted directly while uncertain ones go to a human triage queue. How should they implement this routing?
answers: Instruct the reviewer to report only high-confidence findings so every posted comment can safely be blocking.
Map each finding's severity label to a route, treating critical and high severity as confident enough to post directly.
Run the review pass twice and send to triage any finding that appears in only one of the two runs.
Have the reviewer attach a confidence level to each finding and route on a threshold calibrated against labeled findings.
feedbacks: Instructions to be conservative at the finding stage reduce what gets reported. Real but uncertain issues are dropped without notice instead of being sent to triage. The documented guidance is to ask for every issue, with a confidence level attached, and to filter in a separate pass. It is not to limit what gets reported at the start.

Severity and confidence are independent. A finding can have critical impact and still be very uncertain, such as a suspected but unconfirmed injection path. Routing on severity alone would post the uncertain high-impact findings directly, and those are the findings that most need human triage.

Agreement between runs measures how much the output varies. It does not measure how uncertain the model is about a specific finding. A wrong finding can appear in both runs. This approach also doubles the cost, and it still does not produce the per-finding confidence value that the routing decision needs.

This keeps coverage separate from filtering. The reviewer reports every finding with a confidence value. A separate routing step then decides whether to post the finding directly or send it to human triage. This is the documented verification-pass pattern for routing review findings by confidence. It keeps recall high at the finding stage and still controls what developers see. The routing threshold must be calibrated against findings that developers have already labeled, because a raw self-reported confidence value is often poorly calibrated.
prompt.explanation:
The design principle is to separate coverage from filtering. Suppose you move filtering into the finding stage, for example by telling the reviewer to be conservative or to report only what it is sure about. Then the model reports less, and you cannot see the findings it drops. You cannot triage a finding that was never reported. Anthropic's prompting guidance states this directly for review workloads. Ask the model to report every issue, including uncertain and low-severity ones. Have it attach a confidence level and an estimated severity to each finding, so a later stage can rank, filter, and route them.

The team's requirement belongs in that later step. A self-reported confidence field gives the pipeline a value for each finding that it can act on deterministically. High-confidence findings are posted directly as blocking comments. Low-confidence findings go to a human triage queue. Note that confidence in this design is a field the model produces in your output schema. It is not a calibrated probability that the API computes for you. It is imperfect, and the model can be confidently wrong. So the team must calibrate the routing threshold against a set of findings that developers have already labeled as correct or incorrect. Even then, the routing design sends the uncertain findings to human review instead of dismissing any of them automatically.

Each alternative breaks this separation. Filtering inside the reviewer prompt makes the results look more precise, but it loses findings without any sign that they were lost. Comparing two runs measures sampling variation, not real uncertainty, and two runs can agree and still both be wrong. Severity-based routing mixes up two independent properties. The findings that most need a human to look at them are often the high-severity, low-confidence ones.

See Prompting guidance for code review findings and Reduce hallucinations for related verification-pass patterns.

QUESTION: A nightly batch job submits one code review request per changed file and maps the Nth line of the results file to the Nth submitted request. Reviews occasionally attach to the wrong files. What is the correct fix?
answers: Submit the per-file requests in sorted order so the results file comes back in that same sequence.
Embed the file path in each prompt and parse it back out of the model's generated review text.
Match each result to its originating request using the "custom_id" field instead of line position.
Detect misaligned results after each run and automatically resubmit the whole batch until they align.
feedbacks: The Message Batches API processes each request independently. It states clearly that results are not guaranteed to appear in input order, no matter how the requests were sorted when they were submitted. Sorting the inputs cannot make mapping by position safe.

Depending on the model to repeat an identifier in free text breaks easily. The model may reword the path, cut it short, or leave it out. The API already provides a reliable matching field on every result, so parsing the model's output for this purpose is unnecessary and can cause errors.

Batch results are not guaranteed to come back in the order they were submitted, so mapping by position is unreliable by design. Every result line includes the custom_id that the developer set on the original request. This is the documented way to match each response to its request.

Resubmitting does not change the fact that result order is not guaranteed, so the next run can be misaligned in a different way. Adding retries treats a deterministic matching problem as if it were a temporary failure.
prompt.explanation:
The Message Batches API processes every request in a batch independently and asynchronously. This is what makes the 50% discount possible: Anthropic can schedule the work in the most efficient way within the 24-hour window. As a direct result, the .jsonl results file is not guaranteed to list results in the order the requests were submitted. A pipeline that maps line N of the results to request N depends on an order that the API never promised. This produces the occasional wrong matches described in the scenario.

The designed solution is the custom_id field. Every batch request must include a custom_id chosen by the developer. It must be unique within the batch and be 1 to 64 characters of letters, digits, hyphens, and underscores. Every line in the results file returns this value together with the result. The key idea is a join key. You choose an identifier that has meaning in your system (in this scenario, something based on the file path), and you join results back to inputs on that key. The same key also helps with failure handling. You can see which requests came back as errored or expired and resubmit only those.

Sorting the submissions does nothing, because the API does not guarantee any order. Resubmitting the batch when results are misaligned adds cost and delay, and it does not change the matching logic that is actually broken. Putting the path in the prompt and parsing it from the model's text replaces a deterministic protocol field with probabilistic model behavior. Structured mechanisms exist to avoid this kind of fragility.

See the Message Batches API guide and the batch results reference for details on matching and ordering.

QUESTION: One job in the pipeline defines two tools, "report_review_findings" and "suggest_test_cases", but its downstream parser accepts exactly one review-findings tool call per run. Some runs instead return test suggestions, plain prose, or multiple parallel tool calls. Which configuration guarantees the parser always receives a single review-findings call?
answers: Set "tool_choice" to {"type": "tool", "name": "report_review_findings"} and set "disable_parallel_tool_use" to true.
Set "tool_choice" to {"type": "any"} with "disable_parallel_tool_use" set to true so exactly one tool is called each run.
Keep "tool_choice" at {"type": "auto"} and strengthen the system prompt to always call the review findings tool first.
Enable "strict": true on the review findings tool so schema enforcement guarantees that tool is the one invoked.
feedbacks: Forced tool selection requires Claude to call the specific named tool. Disabling parallel tool use guarantees exactly one tool call per response. Together, these settings remove all three failures: plain-text responses, calls to the wrong tool, and multiple parallel calls.

The "any" setting with parallel tool use disabled guarantees exactly one tool call. But the model still chooses which tool to call, so it could call "suggest_test_cases". This setting removes plain text and multiple calls, but not calls to the wrong tool.

With "auto", the model decides whether to call a tool at all. Prompt instructions only make it more likely that the model follows them; they do not guarantee it. Runs could still return plain text, and the downstream parser cannot accept plain text.

Strict tool use guarantees that when the tool is called, its name and input match the schema. It does not require the model to call that tool, or any tool. So it cannot prevent plain-text responses, calls to the wrong tool, or extra parallel calls.
prompt.explanation:
The tool_choice parameter accepts four values, and each one gives a different guarantee. With {"type": "auto"} (the default when tools are provided), Claude decides whether to call a tool at all. So plain-text responses are still possible, no matter how strongly the prompt asks for a tool call. With {"type": "any"}, Claude must call some tool, but it chooses which one. This is the right setting when several schemas are valid and the model should pick the best match, for example several extraction tools for documents of unknown type. With forced selection, written as {"type": "tool", "name": "..."}, Claude must call that exact tool. This matches this job's requirement that one specific schema is produced on every run. The fourth value, {"type": "none"}, prevents tool use completely and does not apply in this scenario.

The question asks for three guarantees at the same time. A tool call must happen, it must be a particular tool, and it must be the only call. Forced selection gives the first two. But Claude may make multiple tool calls in parallel by default, so disable_parallel_tool_use: true is what limits the response to exactly one call. The "any" setting with parallel use disabled gives one call, but not the right tool. "auto" with stronger prompt wording gives none of the guarantees reliably. strict: true solves a different problem. It makes sure that tool inputs match the declared JSON schema when a call happens, but it never forces a call. When tool_choice is "any" or a forced tool, the API prefills the assistant turn to force tool use. That is why the response comes back as a tool_use block that matches the schema, not as plain text that the parser would have to clean up.

This is why forced tool selection with parallel tool use disabled is the standard pattern for pipeline stages with strict downstream contracts. The API enforces the output shape, so you do not depend on the model choosing to comply. See Define tools for the full tool_choice behavior and Strict tool use for what schema enforcement covers and does not cover.

QUESTION: The pipeline extracts review findings into a tool schema that marks "related_ticket" as required, and Claude invents plausible ticket IDs whenever a pull request description references no ticket. What schema change most reliably prevents these fabricated values?
answers: Change "related_ticket" to a nullable type so Claude can return null when no ticket is referenced.
Validate each extracted ticket ID against the issue tracker and retry the extraction when validation fails.
Add a system prompt instruction stating that ticket identifiers must never be guessed or invented.
Have Claude attach a confidence score to each ticket ID so low-confidence values can be filtered out.
feedbacks: A required, non-nullable field forces Claude to produce some value even when the source contains nothing. This is what causes the invented values. Allowing null gives the model a valid way to report that the value is missing. Missing tickets then appear as null instead of as invented IDs.

Retrying with error feedback works for format and structure mistakes. But it cannot succeed when the information is not in the source at all. A pull request with no ticket reference will fail validation on every retry, because there is no correct value to extract.

A prompt instruction directly conflicts with a schema that still requires a value in every extraction. The schema requires the field, so the model must output something. Following a prompt instruction is probabilistic, and it cannot override this constraint in the schema.

Self-rated confidence is poorly calibrated. It does not stop the invented values from being produced; it only tries to flag them afterward. Invented values can still come with high confidence. The root cause, a schema that does not allow a missing value, also stays in place.
prompt.explanation:
This is a core principle of schema design for extraction. A schema does not only describe the output. It also limits what the model is allowed to say. When a field is required and non-nullable, the model has no valid way to say "this document does not contain that information." So it fills the gap with the most realistic-looking value it can create. Anthropic's documentation warns about this behavior: when a required parameter has no basis in the input, Claude may infer or guess a reasonable value. The fix is in the schema, not in the wording of the prompt. Declare the field with a union type, such as a string that also allows null, or remove it from the required list. Then tell Claude to use null when the source has no evidence. The model now has an honest way to report a missing value. Downstream code can treat null as a meaningful signal instead of trusting an invented ID.

The incorrect approaches all treat symptoms. A prompt rule against guessing asks the model to do something that the schema does not allow, and the schema constraint wins that conflict. A validation-retry loop is the right tool for format errors that the model can correct. But retries do not work when the required information is not in the source. There is no correct answer for the model to reach. Confidence scores only label invented values after they are produced, and self-reported confidence is not reliable enough to separate real tickets from invented ones.

The broader point is this. Structured outputs and tool schemas guarantee syntactic compliance: valid JSON, required fields present, and correct types. They say nothing about whether the values are true. To prevent hallucinated values, design the schema so that a missing value can be represented, and combine it with grounding instructions. See Structured outputs, Tool use overview, and Reduce hallucinations.

QUESTION: A nightly audit step uses Claude to extract vulnerability counts from scanner reports into JSON, which decides whether a pull request can be merged. Some reports contain a summary line whose total disagrees with the list of individual findings, and the extraction silently returns a single value. How should the extraction be redesigned?
answers: Instruct the model in the prompt to report whichever of the conflicting counts it judges more reliable.
Add a validation retry loop that re-prompts the model with the error until the two counts in its output agree.
Extract both the stated total and a total computed from the listed entries, with a boolean flagging mismatches.
Add a numeric constraint to the JSON schema requiring the total field to equal the sum of the listed entries.
feedbacks: Asking the model to choose between conflicting values only moves the hidden choice from the extraction code into the prompt. The disagreement is a data quality signal that the pipeline needs to see. Throwing away one of the values destroys that signal.

Retrying with error feedback fixes format and structure mistakes. In this scenario, though, the source document itself contradicts itself. No number of retries can make the summary line and the list of individual findings agree. The loop would either fail forever or push the model to invent agreement.

The extraction returns a stated_total and a calculated_total, plus a conflict_detected boolean. This shows the inconsistency in the source data instead of hiding it. The downstream merge check can then send conflicting reports for review, instead of acting on a value that was chosen without anyone seeing it.

JSON schemas for structured output cannot express arithmetic rules between fields. The documentation lists numerical constraints such as minimum and multipleOf as unsupported. A schema guarantees the shape of the output, not that its meaning is correct. So an equality rule must be handled in the prompt or in application logic.
prompt.explanation:
This is the standard example for a self-correction validation flow. When a source document can contradict itself, the extraction schema should capture both versions. The extraction returns a stated_total (what the summary line says) and a calculated_total (the sum of the listed entries), plus a conflict_detected boolean. This turns a hidden data quality problem into a clear signal that code can read. When the flag is true, the pipeline can block the merge to be safe or send the report to a human. It does not make merge decisions based on a value that the model picked without telling anyone.

The key idea is the difference between syntactic and semantic guarantees. Structured outputs limit Claude's response to a schema. So you reliably get JSON that can be parsed, with the required fields and types. But nothing in that mechanism checks whether the numbers agree with each other or with the document. You also cannot put arithmetic relationships into the schema. Numerical constraints such as minimum, maximum, and multipleOf are unsupported and produce an error, so the schema has no place for an "equals the sum" rule. Semantic checks belong in the prompt, in the extraction design itself (as in this scenario), or in post-processing code.

The other approaches fail for typical reasons. Retrying with error feedback is a strong pattern for format and structure errors. But the documentation says it does not work when the problem is in the source data. A report that contradicts itself still contradicts itself on the tenth attempt. Letting the model choose the "more reliable" count is a form of averaging or picking between conflicting values. It throws away the disagreement information that a reliable pipeline needs.

See Structured outputs for what schemas support and their limits, and Increase output consistency for related consistency techniques.

QUESTION: Metrics show an automated code reviewer's performance findings are wrong about half the time, while its security findings are over 90% accurate. Developers have begun dismissing findings across all categories without reading them. What should the team do?
answers: Attach the model's self-rated confidence score to each finding so developers can judge which ones to investigate.
Temporarily disable the performance category while its prompts are improved, keeping the accurate categories live.
Make the reviewer less strict in every category to lower the overall false-positive rate.
Keep every category live and rely on the category labels so developers can discount performance findings selectively.
feedbacks: Self-stated confidence is poorly calibrated. Developers still have to sort through incorrect findings, so the cost of investigating them, which is why developers stopped paying attention, stays the same. Confidence scores change the order of the findings, but they do not remove the false positives that are destroying trust.

A high false-positive rate in one category reduces trust in the whole reviewer. So the category with many errors must be removed from what developers see while it is fixed. Disabling it protects the credibility of the security findings, which are 90% accurate. It also gives the team time to improve the performance prompts before turning the category back on.

The problem is concentrated in one category. A reduction in strictness across all categories would hide valid security and correctness findings that are already accurate. Work on precision should focus on the category with many errors. It should not weaken the whole reviewer.

Developers do not keep a separate level of trust for each category. When one category is wrong half the time, developers learn that the reviewer in general is unreliable, and they start dismissing the accurate categories too. The scenario shows this is already happening, so labels alone cannot limit the damage.
prompt.explanation:
Developer trust in an automated reviewer is one shared resource. It is not tracked separately for each category. Developers quickly form a simple general judgment from recent experience. If about half of what the reviewer says turns out to be wrong, they conclude "this tool is unreliable," not "this tool's performance category is unreliable." That is why a 50% false-positive rate in one category reduces engagement with the security findings, which are 90% accurate. The dismissal behavior spreads across the whole system, and the scenario confirms that this has already happened. The right step is to treat the category with many errors as something that damages the other categories. Turn it off, improve its prompts with explicit criteria for what to report and what to skip, and turn it back on once its precision improves.

This is also why Anthropic's managed Code Review pipeline includes an explicit verification stage. This stage checks candidate findings against the code again and filters out false positives before anything is posted. Its customization guidance (through REVIEW.md) also stresses skipping types of findings that produce many errors, or requiring evidence before they are reported. Each false positive costs the author time to check and respond, and it slowly reduces the credibility of every future finding.

The alternatives misunderstand how trust works. Category labels do not protect the accurate categories. The developer pays the cost of investigating a finding before knowing whether the finding was correct. Self-rated confidence scores are poorly calibrated and leave the work of triage with developers. A reduction in strictness across all categories penalizes the categories that work well. It hides real security findings to make up for a problem that is in a different category. See Code Review and Customize Code Review for how verification and review instructions stop false positives from damaging trust in the whole system.

QUESTION: The pipeline extracts structured ticket metadata from each pull request description, validates the result against a JSON schema, and retries failures with the validation error attached. Which TWO statements about this retry loop are accurate? (Select TWO.)
answers: Sending back the specific validation error typically fixes format and structural mistakes within a retry or two.
Raising the retry limit from two attempts to five eventually recovers values that are missing from the source.
Having the model rate its own confidence on each retry resolves persistent validation failures.
No number of retries can produce a value that is simply absent from the submitted PR description.
feedbacks: Retrying with specific error feedback is the documented pattern for correcting format and structure problems. Examples are a date in the wrong format or a value placed in the wrong field. When the model gets the original document and the exact error, it usually corrects itself in one or two attempts.

Adding more retries does not change what the source document contains. A value that is really missing stays missing. Extra attempts, with pressure to satisfy the schema, increase the risk of an invented value. They do not increase the chance of a correct one.

Self-rated confidence can help decide which outputs to send for review. But it does not correct the extraction itself. A failure that keeps happening because the source is missing information stays unsolved, no matter how the model scores its own certainty.

Retries only let the model look at the same source again. If the required information is not in the document, asking again cannot create it. The right handling is to allow a null or an explicit "unknown" value, instead of pressuring the model to fill the field.
prompt.explanation:
The validation-retry loop is a core reliability pattern for structured extraction. The application validates Claude's output against a schema (and business rules). When validation fails, it sends a new prompt with the original document, the incorrect extraction, and the specific validation error. The specific error is important. An error like "field total is 150 but line items sum to 145" gives the model something concrete to check again. That is why format mistakes, fields in the wrong place, and arithmetic inconsistencies are usually fixed within one or two retries.

The important limit is what the retry can work with. A retry lets the model look at the same source again with better guidance. It cannot create information that the source never contained. If a PR description does not include the ticket number, no number of retries fixes that. Requiring the field anyway encourages the model to invent a value. Anthropic's hallucination guidance addresses this directly. Give Claude explicit permission to say that the information is not present. Design schemas with nullable or optional fields, so missing data becomes a null instead of an invented value (see Reduce hallucinations).

The incorrect options make the same mistake. They treat more retries or self-assessment as a replacement for missing evidence. More attempts only try again on the same source, which still does not contain the value. Self-rated confidence is a signal for routing, not a way to correct anything. Schema enforcement has a similar limit. It guarantees the syntactic shape of the output, but not that the source is complete or that the facts are correct (see Structured outputs). The design lesson is to classify failures first. Retry the ones that can be fixed, with error feedback. Report the ones that cannot be fixed as clear gaps, so they can go to upstream retrieval or human review.

QUESTION: A review-summary extraction step uses a validation-retry loop, and most failures resolve within two retries. One required field, the linked ticket's acceptance criteria, fails on every retry because that information exists only in the issue tracker, not in the pull request diff sent to Claude. What change resolves this failure class?
answers: Strengthen the prompt to state that the acceptance criteria field is mandatory and must never be empty.
Have Claude self-rate confidence per field and accept its lowest-confidence guess after the final retry.
Raise the retry limit from two to five and include fuller validation errors on each attempt.
Include the ticket's acceptance criteria from the issue tracker in the request context before extraction.
feedbacks: If the source does not contain the information, insisting more strongly on a required field pushes the model to invent a realistic-looking value. The visible validation failure becomes a hidden hallucination. This is worse for downstream systems.

Self-rated confidence does not create information that the model never received. Any value produced for the missing field would be invented. Accepting a guess puts invented data into the pipeline instead of fixing the root cause.

More retries with more detailed error feedback help when the model formatted or placed data wrongly, and that data is visible to it. No number of retries lets the model produce acceptance criteria that were never provided in its context.

Retries only succeed when the model can correct a format or structure mistake using information it already has. In this scenario, the required data never reached the model. The fix is to supply the missing source material. After that, the extraction can succeed on the first attempt.
prompt.explanation:
The main point of this question is which extraction failures a validation-retry loop can fix. Retrying with error feedback works when the model's mistake is about form. Examples are invalid JSON syntax, a value in the wrong field, a date in the wrong format, or an arithmetic inconsistency that the model can check again. In these cases, the information is present in the context. A specific error message (for example, "field total is 150 but line items sum to 145, re-check values") gives the model everything it needs to correct itself, usually within one or two attempts.

Retries cannot work when the required information is not in the provided source. The acceptance criteria are stored in an external issue tracker that was never included in the request. So every retry asks the model to produce data that it has no way of knowing. The documented fix is to change the input, not to repeat the request. Fetch the ticket and include its content in the context (or give the model a tool to retrieve it) before the extraction runs. Anthropic's guardrail guidance supports the same principle from the other side. When answers must come from provided documents, the model should be allowed to report that there is not enough information. It should not be pressured into filling a gap, because that pressure produces hallucinated values. That is why requiring the field to be "mandatory and never empty" and accepting a low-confidence guess are both anti-patterns in this scenario. Both turn an honest failure that you can detect into invented data that looks confident and flows to downstream systems.

See Reduce Hallucinations for grounding answers in provided source material, and Tool Use Overview for providing external data that the model needs through tools.

QUESTION: You are writing a SKILL.md for a skill that finds missing tests in CI and produces thousands of lines of exploratory output. Which two implementation choices should you make? (Select TWO.)
answers: Write all context the task needs into the skill itself, since a forked skill starts with no history.
Set "context: fork" in the frontmatter so the verbose exploration runs in an isolated subagent.
Keep the skill brief and rely on the fork inheriting the session's prior messages for task details.
Omit "allowed-tools" because "context: fork" already restricts the subagent to read-only operations.
feedbacks: A forked skill is not a fork of the current conversation. The subagent does not see the earlier conversation history. It receives only the skill content as its prompt. The documentation states clearly that the skill must include all the context needed to complete the task.

This is the purpose of context: fork. Claude Code starts a subagent, and the skill content becomes its prompt. The long exploratory output stays in the subagent's own context. The main conversation receives only the short final result. This solves the problem of the main context filling up with exploration output.

Inheriting the conversation history describes a conversation fork. That is a different mechanism from a forked skill. A skill with context: fork starts a new subagent that receives only the skill content as its prompt. So a skill that depends on earlier messages will run without the context it expects.

Tool restrictions come from the allowed-tools field in the frontmatter (the settings block at the top of the file) or from the chosen subagent type. They do not come from context: fork. Setting context: fork changes where the skill runs, not which tools it is allowed to use.
prompt.explanation:
The context: fork option in the frontmatter (the settings block at the top of the file) exists to keep high-volume work out of the main session. When a skill with this setting is invoked, Claude Code starts a subagent and passes the skill's content to it as the prompt. The subagent then does its exploration in its own context window. Thousands of lines of search results, file contents, and intermediate reasoning build up inside the fork. Only the final result goes back into the main conversation. For a CI skill that finds missing tests, this keeps room in the main context for the review feedback that actually matters.

A forked skill is not a fork of the conversation. The subagent starts fresh and never sees the user's earlier messages. That is why the documentation says the skill must include everything the task needs. It is also why context: fork only makes sense for skills with explicit, self-contained instructions, not for skills that only provide reference guidance. If a task really depends on what was discussed earlier in the session, a conversation fork (which inherits the whole conversation) is the right mechanism instead.

A skill designed to depend on inherited conversation history mixes up these two mechanisms. The result is a skill that runs without the context it expects, and nothing reports the problem. Leaving out allowed-tools because you assume the fork enforces read-only access mixes up isolated execution with permission control. Tool access is controlled by allowed-tools in the frontmatter, or by the subagent type selected with the agent field (for example, combining context: fork with the read-only Explore agent for codebase analysis). See Claude Code Skills and Subagents for the full behavior.

QUESTION: The team plans to use the Message Batches API overnight to generate test-case suggestions for 8,000 legacy modules, using a newly written prompt that has never been run at scale. What should they do before submitting the full batch?
answers: Rewrite the prompt with stronger, more emphatic instructions about accuracy before launching the full batch.
Run the prompt synchronously on a representative sample of modules, iterating until outputs meet quality criteria.
Submit the entire batch now and use "custom_id" values to identify and resubmit any requests that fail.
Add an automated retry loop that resubmits each unsatisfactory batch result with its validation error attached.
feedbacks: Stronger wording without testing gives no evidence that the prompt actually works well on real inputs. General emphasis, such as stressing accuracy, does not give the model concrete criteria to follow. The team would still be running an untested prompt on 8,000 modules.

Testing and improving the prompt on a small, representative sample before scaling up gives the full batch the best chance of success on the first run. Synchronous testing gives fast feedback. A batch test cycle can take up to 24 hours for each attempt, so trial and error at large scale is slow and expensive.

The custom_id field is the right mechanism for matching results and resubmitting requests that actually failed. But it is a recovery tool, not a quality strategy. If prompt weaknesses are found only after an 8,000-request batch completes, each improvement cycle can take up to 24 hours. The team also pays for thousands of low-quality outputs.

Retrying with error feedback is effective for correcting individual format or structure failures. But it handles the effects of a weak prompt one output at a time. If the prompt itself produces consistently poor suggestions, retrying at scale increases the cost. It does not fix the root cause before the batch runs.
prompt.explanation:
Large batch jobs multiply whatever quality the prompt already has. If a prompt produces low-quality test suggestions on ten modules, it will produce low-quality suggestions on 8,000, and the team pays for all of them. Because of how the Message Batches API is priced and timed, improving the prompt before submission is the most important step. A batch can take up to 24 hours to complete. So every improvement cycle at full scale costs a day of waiting and the price of thousands of wasted completions. Running the new prompt synchronously on a representative sample reverses this. Feedback arrives in minutes. The prompt is tuned against real inputs, including edge cases. Only then is the 50% batch discount applied, to a prompt that is known to work. Anthropic's batch guidance states this directly: it recommends a test run of a request shape with the synchronous Messages API before batching. Its prompting guidance also recommends testing prompts against a subset of test cases to confirm quality improvements before scaling up.

The other approaches all wait to check quality until after the money is spent. Using custom_id to resubmit failures is essential for matching results and recovering from real request errors. But it does nothing about outputs that succeed technically but are low quality. An automated retry loop with validation errors is a documented pattern for fixing individual format or structure mistakes. When the prompt is consistently weak, though, the loop only increases cost across the whole batch. Strengthening the prompt's wording without testing it is a common trap: it uses emphasis in place of evidence. You find out whether a prompt is good by running it, not by how strongly it is worded.

See Batch processing and Prompting guidance for Claude Sonnet for the documented best practices.

QUESTION: A team's Agent SDK tool generates refactoring changes across a service, then runs an automated review step before opening a pull request. The review must not be influenced by the reasoning that produced the changes. How should the reviewer be set up?
answers: Delegate to a standard subagent, passing the diff, affected files, and review criteria in its prompt.
Have the generating agent attach a confidence score to each change and show reviewers only the low-confidence ones.
Fork the generating session so the reviewer starts with the files and decisions already in context.
Resume the generating agent and instruct it to critique its own changes against the review criteria.
feedbacks: A standard subagent (not a fork) starts with a fresh, isolated context window. It does not see the parent conversation or the generator's reasoning. Only the delegation prompt is passed to it. So the diff, the relevant files, and the review criteria must be included explicitly. This gives the reviewer everything it needs and keeps it independent.

Self-rated confidence comes from the same context that produced the changes, and it is poorly calibrated. Changes that the generator confidently justified would never be reviewed. Those are the changes that most need an independent check.

A fork inherits the parent conversation, including the reasoning and decisions that produced the changes. That convenience brings back the generator's justifications, so the review is no longer independent.

A resumed agent keeps its full conversation history, including earlier tool calls and reasoning. Self-critique in that context stays tied to the conclusions the generator already reached, so it rarely challenges them.
prompt.explanation:
This scenario requires a review that is not influenced by the reasoning that produced the code. This matches the context isolation property of subagents. A standard subagent (not a fork) runs as a separate Claude instance with its own clean context window. It does not see the parent conversation, the files the generator already read, or the generator's earlier tool results. The delegation prompt is the only content the parent passes to it. So the reviewer must receive the diff, the affected files, and explicit review criteria in that prompt. Without the generator's justifications, the reviewer has to work out again whether each change is safe. This is how an independent reviewer catches issues that the author wrongly justified.

The other setups all let the generator's context leak into the review. A fork inherits the parent conversation by design. Starting with everything already in context looks efficient, but it is what destroys independence. Resuming the generating agent keeps its full history, including the reasoning that justified the original decisions. Stricter critique instructions cannot remove the bias that this history creates. Self-rated confidence scores are produced inside the same biased context and are poorly calibrated. So the changes that the generator justified confidently, which most need careful checking, would skip review completely. When you define the reviewer, it is also good practice to limit it to read-only tools such as Read, Grep, and Glob. This matches Anthropic's documented code-reviewer pattern.

See Claude Code subagents for context isolation, forks, and reviewer tool restrictions, and Agent SDK subagents for defining reviewers in code and for what content actually passes from parent to subagent.

QUESTION: During a multi-phase refactoring task, the team spawns investigation subagents, but each one returns full file contents plus its step-by-step reasoning, rapidly consuming the main conversation's context window. What change addresses this most effectively?
answers: Instruct the main agent in CLAUDE.md to disregard irrelevant detail when reading subagent reports.
Have each subagent return structured findings: key facts, file paths, and relevance, not raw content.
Switch the main conversation to a model with a larger context window and keep accumulating reports.
Run /compact after each subagent completes so its verbose report is summarized before the next one starts.
feedbacks: An instruction to ignore content does not remove that content from the context window. The long file contents and reasoning still use tokens and reduce the model's attention to what matters. Instructions cannot undo the growth of context that is already loaded into the conversation.

This fixes the output format where the output is produced, so the long exploration output never enters the main context at all. Subagents run in isolated contexts. The raw files and reasoning stay with them, and only short, useful results go back to the coordinator.

A larger window only delays the same loss of quality, at a higher cost. Accuracy and recall still go down as the token count grows. The problem is what enters the context, not how much the window can hold.

Compaction responds only after the long reports have already filled the window. Its summaries can also lose specific details, such as exact file paths and numbers. It treats the effect, while the subagents keep producing the oversized output that caused it.
prompt.explanation:
In multi-agent and subagent workflows, space in the main conversation is limited. Subagents run in isolated contexts. So long exploration, long file reads, and intermediate reasoning can all happen in a separate thread that is thrown away when the task finishes. The only thing that stays in the coordinator's window is what the subagent returns. So the most effective fix is to change what the subagent is required to return. Require short, structured results (key facts, file paths, and relevance assessments) instead of raw content and chains of reasoning. This fixes the root cause instead of cleaning up afterwards.

The incorrect approaches all have the same flaw: they act after the context has already grown too large. Running /compact again and again compresses history that should never have built up, and summaries can lose exact identifiers that the refactoring phases depend on. A larger context window only delays the loss of quality. Anthropic states that recall and accuracy go down as context grows (this is sometimes called context rot), no matter what the stated limit is. An instruction in CLAUDE.md to ignore detail changes nothing about token use. Every byte of a long report still counts toward the window and competes for the model's attention.

The key idea is to treat each subagent boundary as an interface with a defined, minimal output schema, the same way you would design an API response. Everything in a request counts toward the context window, including tool results and earlier messages. So choosing carefully what passes between agents is the main way to manage context. See Manage tool context, Context windows, and Multi-agent orchestration.

QUESTION: A developer gave Claude Code three input/output test cases while asking it to implement a date-normalization function. The generated code contains branches matching those exact inputs and fails on other valid date formats. What prompt change most effectively fixes this?
answers: Replace the test cases with a detailed prose description of the normalization rules.
Have Claude rate its confidence for each supported input format and retry the low-confidence conversions.
Ask for a general-purpose solution that treats the test cases as verification, not the full specification.
Add another example to the prompt each time a new failing input appears in production.
feedbacks: Concrete input/output examples are a documented strength for explaining transformations. Removing them loses that clarity. Written descriptions of format rules are often interpreted inconsistently. So this replaces one reliability problem with another and does not fix the hardcoding behavior.

Self-rated confidence is unreliable, because a model can be confident and wrong. Retrying does not change code that was written to match specific inputs. The problem is in how the implementation was specified, not in uncertainty at run time.

Claude can focus too much on passing the test cases it was given and hardcode logic for those exact inputs. The documented fix for this problem is to ask explicitly for a general-purpose implementation that works for all valid inputs, and to say that the examples are only for checking behavior.

This approach only reacts to failures and never fixes the root cause: Claude treats the set of examples as the complete specification. Each new example can produce one more hardcoded branch. Every input format that has not yet appeared in production stays unhandled.
prompt.explanation:
Concrete input/output examples are one of the most effective ways to explain a transformation to Claude. But they have a known risk: the model can focus too much on passing the supplied cases. It then produces code that handles those exact inputs as special cases, instead of implementing the general rule. Anthropic's prompting guidance addresses this directly. Ask for a general-purpose solution that works for all valid inputs, and present the test cases as a way to verify correctness, not as the definition of the solution. The examples then do what they are good at: they define the expected format without ambiguity. The instruction tells Claude what the examples are for.

Examples and instructions have different roles in a prompt. Examples show what correct behavior looks like. Instructions define the scope of the task. When examples appear without a statement of scope, the model may infer the narrowest pattern that fits them. That is the hardcoding behavior seen in this scenario. Adding an example for every production failure never solves this, because each new example can become one more branch. Self-rated confidence with retries targets uncertainty at run time, not a specification problem that is built into the generated code. Replacing the examples with a written description loses the clarity that examples give. Written rules for date formats are interpreted inconsistently, and examples exist to solve that problem.

See Claude prompting best practices for the guidance on general-purpose solutions and treating tests as verification, and Claude Code common workflows for prompting for specific behavior in tests and for edge cases.

QUESTION: Your monorepo has a packages/mobile/ directory whose coding conventions differ from the rest of the codebase. Teammates should receive these conventions automatically whenever they work on mobile files, without the conventions loading into unrelated sessions. Where should the conventions live?
answers: In each developer's ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md, with a note to apply them only to mobile code.
In a skill under .claude/skills/ that developers invoke before editing mobile code.
In a CLAUDE.md file inside packages/mobile/, committed to the repository.
In a clearly labeled section of the root CLAUDE.md so every session can see them.
feedbacks: User-level configuration is personal. It applies across all of that developer's projects and is never shared through version control. Each teammate would have to copy and maintain the conventions by hand. The copies would become different over time, and the team would not receive the conventions automatically.

Skills are on-demand workflows. They only take effect when someone remembers to invoke them. This makes conventions that should always apply optional and easy to forget. Conventions that should guide every edit in a directory belong in a memory file that loads automatically for that work.

A directory-level CLAUDE.md is the documented mechanism for conventions that belong to one specific part of the codebase. It is shared through version control. Claude Code loads it only when files in that subdirectory are read or edited. So unrelated sessions never have the mobile conventions in their context.

The root project CLAUDE.md loads at the start of every session, whatever the task is. So the mobile conventions would take up context even in sessions that never touch mobile code. This directly breaks the requirement that the conventions must not load into unrelated sessions.
prompt.explanation:
Claude Code's memory system is a hierarchy of CLAUDE.md files. User-level instructions at ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md apply to one person across all projects. Project-level instructions at the repository root (or .claude/CLAUDE.md) hold conventions the whole team should always see. Directory-level CLAUDE.md files inside subdirectories hold conventions for one area of the codebase. Location sets scope: where a file is stored decides who receives it and when it enters the context.

Directory-level files have a property that matters in monorepos: they are lazy-loaded. Claude Code does not load every subdirectory's CLAUDE.md into context when the session starts. It loads one only after Claude reads, writes, or edits a file in that subdirectory. This is a deliberate design choice. In large repositories where most sessions touch only a small part of the code, it keeps the context small. It still guarantees that the relevant conventions are present as soon as work actually enters that area. Committing the file to the repository means every teammate gets it when they clone or pull, with no setup on each machine.

Each of the other locations breaks one of the stated requirements. The root CLAUDE.md loads into every session. So rules for one area would use context everywhere and compete for attention with the standards that apply to all code. Returning empty results marked as successful is the most harmful pattern. It turns "the lookup broke" into "the ticket does not exist", so the model continues confidently with false information.

QUESTION: An MCP tool this team added returns a JSON payload with 50+ fields on every call, though only five of them matter for the debugging workflow. During long sessions these results accumulate and response quality degrades. What is the most effective fix?
answers: Add a CLAUDE.md rule instructing Claude to disregard the irrelevant result fields.
Run /compact after every few tool calls so summaries keep the context lean.
Enable prompt caching so the repeated verbose tool results cost fewer tokens.
Change the tool to return only the fields the debugging workflow uses.
feedbacks: An instruction to ignore fields does not remove them from the context. All 50+ fields still enter the window and use tokens on every call. The loss of quality comes from this buildup, and instructions alone cannot prevent it.

Compaction treats the effect after the extra content has already entered the context. Summaries can also drop exact details, such as specific values and identifiers. Compaction helps a window that is already full. It does not fix tool outputs that are too long by design.
Prompt caching reduces the cost of repeated tokens. It does not reduce how many tokens are in the context window. The long results would still build up and lower response quality in long sessions.

Reducing the tool output where it is produced keeps irrelevant fields from ever entering the conversation. This fixes the root cause. Tool results no longer use far more context tokens than their relevance justifies. So long sessions stay usable without a later cleanup that loses information.
prompt.explanation:
Tool results are one of the most common reasons that context grows too large in agentic workflows. A tool that returns 50+ fields when only five are relevant wastes tokens on every call. Over a long session, this waste adds up until the model pays less attention to the material that matters. The design principle is to reduce long tool outputs before they enter the context. This means fixing the tool interface itself (or intercepting its result) so that only the fields the workflow needs are ever sent back to the model. Everything in a request counts toward the context window, including every tool result that has built up. So the only real fix is to reduce what enters it. See Context windows.

Each incorrect approach misses this root cause. Running /compact compresses history that is already in the window. Summaries lose information, so exact values can be lost. Compaction helps a session recover, but it does not stop the next hundred long results from arriving. Prompt caching is documented as a cost optimization, not a way to reduce context. Cached tokens are cheaper, but they still take up space in the window, as explained in Manage tool context. A CLAUDE.md instruction to ignore fields is guidance about how to read the data. It is not a mechanism that removes the data. The tokens are used whether or not the model pays attention to them.

Context is a budget, and you spend it at the moment data enters the conversation. Changes that act at that point (returning only relevant fields, or having tools return structured summaries instead of raw data) are always more effective than changes that try to clean up or reduce the importance of data after it has already entered.

QUESTION: The team is sorting its backlog by execution style. Which two tasks are good candidates for direct execution rather than plan mode? (Select TWO.)
answers: Migrate the codebase to a new HTTP client library, touching more than 45 files.
Fix an off-by-one bug in one file, pinpointed by a clear stack trace.
Split a shared module into separate services, with several viable boundary designs to weigh.
Add a single input validation check to one function whose behavior is already understood.
feedbacks: A migration across dozens of files has a broad scope and architectural effects. This is the documented case for plan mode. Doing it directly risks expensive rework if the chosen approach turns out to be wrong partway through.

A clear stack trace already shows that the problem is in one file. So there is nothing left to explore and no approach to choose. Simple, well-scoped fixes like this are the documented case for direct execution.

When several possible approaches exist and boundaries must be decided, it is very useful to design before making changes. This task needs plan mode, so the approach can be explored and reviewed before any code changes.

A single validation check in one known function is a small, well-understood change with an obvious approach. For this kind of task, plan mode would add extra work without reducing risk. So direct execution is appropriate.
prompt.explanation:
The choice between direct execution and plan mode depends on how well the change is already understood. In plan mode, Claude researches in a read-only way and proposes an implementation plan for approval before it edits any source files. That review step is valuable when the scope is large, the code is unfamiliar, or several approaches compete. For a change whose diff you could describe in one sentence, the same step is only extra work. Anthropic's guidance is clear on both sides. Small, clear fixes (a typo, a log line, a single validation) should be done directly. Planning is useful when you are unsure about the approach, when the change covers many files, or when you do not know the code being changed.

In this backlog, the single validation check and the off-by-one bug located by the stack trace both have a clear scope and one obvious approach. Each affects about one file. So direct execution finishes them fastest without adding risk. The library migration across 45+ files and the split into services are on the other side of the line. For the migration, the cost of a wrong approach is multiplied across every file it touches. The module split has several possible designs that should be compared before any code is written. Revising a plan is much cheaper than cleaning up after a large change made with the wrong approach. That is why the recommended full workflow separates exploration and planning from implementation, instead of requiring planning for everything.

See Claude Code Best Practices for the guidance on direct execution and planning, and Permission Modes for how plan mode limits Claude to research and a proposal until a plan is approved.

QUESTION: A team's CI script runs "claude -p" with "--output-format json" and a valid JSON Schema supplied via "--json-schema". A jq step reads the ".result" field but gets conversational prose instead of data matching the schema. What should the script do instead?
answers: Wrap the command in a retry loop that reruns it until the "result" field parses as valid JSON.
Switch to "--output-format stream-json", where each event arrives as parseable JSON.
Keep reading the "result" field and add a prompt instruction telling Claude to reply with raw JSON only.
Read the "structured_output" field, where the CLI places the schema-validated data.
feedbacks: Retrying does not change the structure of the response. The result field holds the text answer on every run, and the validated data is in a separate field. A retry loop adds cost and delay, and the script still reads the wrong field.

Stream-json sends step-by-step events during the run, not a final result validated against the schema. It changes how the output is delivered, not where the data that matches the schema is placed. So the script would still not find validated data in the result field.

Prompt instructions only make it more likely that Claude complies; they do not guarantee it. The result field is defined to hold the text answer inside the JSON envelope. The CLI already produces guaranteed schema-validated data in another part of the response. Depending on prompt wording ignores the enforcement that the flags provide.

When the command runs with a JSON schema, the CLI returns the validated data in the structured_output field of the JSON envelope. The result field still holds the agent's text answer. Changing the jq step to read structured_output gives the pipeline the data that matches the schema.
prompt.explanation:
To use Claude Code's structured output in automation, you need to understand the shape of the response envelope. The --output-format json flag does not reformat the model's answer. It wraps the whole run in a JSON object. This object contains metadata (session ID, cost fields, usage) and a result field that holds the agent's text answer. By itself, this gives a script a reliable envelope structure, but no guarantee about the format of the answer inside it.

Adding --json-schema is what adds enforcement. After the agent completes its workflow, the CLI validates the final output against the supplied JSON Schema. It places the data that matches the schema in a separate structured_output field. So a script that keeps parsing result sees what this team saw: conversational prose (ordinary sentences, not structured data), even though the validated data is in a different field. Reliable CI code should also treat a success response that has no structured_output value as a failure. The documented pattern checks both conditions before using the data.

The other approaches miss this design. Switching to stream-json delivers the output as a stream of events. It does not produce a different final payload. Prompt instructions to return raw JSON depend on probabilistic compliance, when a deterministic mechanism already exists. A retry loop around result gets the same envelope structure on every attempt. See Run Claude Code programmatically and the CLI reference for the documented fields and flags.

QUESTION: The team has Claude Code generate docstrings and API reference entries across a large codebase, but technical writers can review only about one fifth of the output. How should the team decide which generated items receive human review?
answers: Output per-item confidence scores, calibrate a review threshold on labeled data, and route low-confidence items to reviewers.
Automate approval entirely for every item, since the pipeline's measured aggregate accuracy already exceeds the team's quality bar.
Validate each generated item against a JSON schema and route only the items that fail validation to human reviewers.
Send a uniform random sample covering one fifth of the generated docstrings and reference entries to reviewers each week.
feedbacks: Confidence scores for each item, calibrated against a labeled validation set, let the team use its limited reviewer time where it helps most: on the items the model is least sure about. This is the documented pattern for deciding which items get human review when there is not enough capacity to review everything.

Overall accuracy can hide poor performance on specific modules, file types, or fields. So a strong overall number does not justify removing human review. Accuracy must be checked for each segment before reducing oversight. Even then, some review capacity should remain to find new error patterns.

Schema validation catches structure problems, such as missing fields or badly formed output. But it cannot detect content with the wrong meaning, such as a docstring that describes a function's behavior incorrectly. Items that pass the schema can still contain the errors that human reviewers are needed to catch.

A purely uniform random sample treats every item as equally likely to be wrong. So most reviewer time goes to items that the model handled correctly. Random sampling is useful as an extra audit to find new error patterns. But it does not put the items most likely to need correction first.
prompt.explanation:
When reviewers can check only part of the model's output, the main design question is how to focus that capacity on the items most likely to be wrong. The documented pattern is confidence-based routing. Have the model output a confidence score for each generated item. Then use a labeled validation set to calibrate the threshold at which items go to humans. Calibration is what makes the scores trustworthy. A raw self-rating has no meaning until you have measured, on labeled examples, how often items at each score level are actually correct. Anthropic's content moderation guide shows the same idea with tiered risk levels. Clear cases are handled automatically, and borderline cases are flagged for human review.

Each incorrect approach misses part of this design. A uniform random sample spends most of its budget on items the model already handles well. Stratified sampling of high-confidence output is a valuable addition for finding new error patterns, but it does not decide which items to review first. Fully automating because the overall accuracy looks good is a known trap. An overall number like 97% can hide much worse performance on a particular module or field type. So accuracy must be checked for each segment before human review is reduced. Finally, JSON schema validation checks shape, not truth. As the structured outputs documentation makes clear, matching the schema prevents badly formed output and missing fields. It does not check that the content is factually correct, and that is what human reviewers are there to judge.
