QUESTION: The agent invokes the MCP tool "mcp__ci__run_tests" (called "run_tests" below) for nearly any request mentioning tests, including requests to locate test files, even though every tool description is detailed and distinct. The system prompt contains: "CRITICAL: You MUST use run_tests whenever testing is mentioned." What change most directly fixes the misrouting?
answers: Reduce the agent's overall tool catalog so "run_tests" competes with fewer alternatives at selection time.
Expand the "run_tests" description with boundary language distinguishing executing tests from locating test files.
Replace the all-caps MUST rule with calm wording that says when tests actually need to run.
Add few-shot routing examples to the system prompt showing when Glob should be used instead of "run_tests".
feedbacks: Reducing an oversized tool catalog improves tool selection when the agent has too many tools to choose from. But that is not the failure in this scenario. The agent is not confused by a large number of tools. It is following an instruction, triggered by a keyword, that requires one specific tool whenever a word appears.

Boundary language in descriptions is the right fix when two tools have overlapping or vague descriptions. But the question states that the descriptions are already detailed and distinct. The root cause in this scenario is a mandatory system prompt instruction based on a keyword. It will keep forcing the tool call, however precise the description becomes.

The wrong tool choices are caused by a strongly worded system prompt instruction that reacts to the word test, whatever the user intends. It overrides tool descriptions that are otherwise good. Anthropic's guidance is to replace wording like "CRITICAL: You MUST use this tool when..." with normal wording such as "Use this tool when...". This removes the forced link to the keyword, and it still guides tool use correctly.

Few-shot examples add tokens, and they only guide the model probabilistically through patterns. They would compete with an explicit mandatory instruction in the same system prompt. Removing or rewording the conflicting keyword instruction fixes the cause directly, instead of adding examples on top of it.
prompt.explanation:
When tools are passed to Claude, the API builds a combined tool-use system prompt from the tool definitions, the tool configuration, and the system prompt that the user supplies. This means the system prompt is in the same context as the tool descriptions, and Claude reads both when it selects a tool. An instruction written in the system prompt can create unintended links to keywords that override even excellent descriptions. A directive like CRITICAL: You MUST use run_tests whenever testing is mentioned links a tool (in this scenario, the MCP tool mcp__ci__run_tests) to a keyword in the request, not to what the user wants. So a request to find test files (a job for Glob) still triggers test execution.

Anthropic warns directly that strong wording, written to fix a tool that is not called often enough, often makes the tool get called too often (over-triggering). It recommends replacing "MUST/CRITICAL" wording with normal language based on intent, such as "Use this tool when the engineer asks to execute tests." With the forced link removed, the well-written descriptions can work as the main way of selecting tools. (In direct Messages API integrations, tool_choice also lets you require that a tool is called, when a call must happen and should not only be encouraged.)

Each of the other approaches solves a different problem. Boundary language in descriptions fixes overlap between descriptions, and the scenario rules that out. Few-shot routing examples give probabilistic hints that still lose to an explicit requirement in the same prompt. Reducing the tool catalog fixes worse selection caused by too many tools, not a fixed keyword trigger. A good habit is to check system prompts for instructions triggered by keywords whenever wrong tool choices continue despite good descriptions.

See Claude prompting best practices, Tool use overview, and Define tools.

QUESTION: A coordinator agent delegates legacy-system investigations to subagents using a prompt that lists eight numbered tool-call steps. Investigations fail whenever a codebase's layout differs from the structure those steps assume. How should the coordinator prompt be revised?
answers: State the investigation goal and the quality criteria the final report must meet, letting the agent choose its steps.
Expand the numbered procedure with conditional branches covering every repository layout the team expects to encounter.
Add a PreToolUse hook that blocks any tool call issued outside the prescribed step order.
Add few-shot examples showing the exact tool-call sequence that succeeded on one representative codebase.
feedbacks: A prompt that states the goal and the quality criteria lets the agent adapt its tool use to the actual structure of each codebase. A fixed step list cannot do this. Anthropic's guidance is to prefer general instructions over prescriptive steps. Numbered sequences should be used only when the order of the steps really matters.

Listing every layout makes the prompt longer and more fragile. It still breaks the first time the agent meets a structure that nobody expected. The cause of the failure is too much prescription, so adding more prescription does not fix the root cause.

Hooks provide deterministic enforcement for critical business rules, such as compliance thresholds. They are not meant for open-ended exploration. Enforcing the broken step order in code would make the process even less flexible. The investigation would then always fail on codebases that the sequence does not fit.

Examples of a fixed tool-call sequence teach the agent to copy that sequence. This produces the same rigid behavior in a different form. Few-shot examples are useful for making the expected output clear. They should not be used to force exploration into one fixed procedure.
prompt.explanation:
In this scenario, the coordinator prompt is written as a fixed procedure, but the task is an open-ended investigation. Legacy codebases have different structures. Any tool-call script written by a person contains assumptions, and those assumptions will not be true for every codebase. Anthropic's prompting guidance is clear on this point. Use sequential numbered steps only when the order or completeness of the steps really matters. Otherwise, prefer general instructions over prescriptive steps. The reason is that the model's own reasoning about the situation in front of it can do better than a plan written in advance.

The effective revision states the goal, which is the question the investigation must answer. It also states the quality criteria, which describe what a complete, well-supported report looks like. The agent then decides for itself whether to start with Grep, Glob, or a directory listing, based on what it finds. The same design principle is behind dynamic adaptive decomposition. When the full scope is not known at the start, each step should be chosen from the results of the previous step, not decided in advance. Goal-oriented prompts also work well with success criteria, such as citing specific files and checking findings in more than one location. These criteria give the agent something it can check, without limiting how it does the work.

The other approaches all add more prescription. Listing repository layouts in conditional branches only delays the next unexpected case. Few-shot examples of one successful tool-call sequence teach the agent to copy that sequence instead of adapting. A PreToolUse hook would change rigid behavior that is likely but not guaranteed (probabilistic) into rigid behavior that is certain (guaranteed). Hooks are the right tool when a rule must never be broken, such as blocking a dangerous action or enforcing a financial threshold. An exploratory workflow needs the opposite.

See Claude prompting best practices for the guidance on general versus prescriptive instructions and on research success criteria, and Subagents in the SDK for how delegation prompts give goals and context to subagents.

QUESTION: An agent endpoint uses "tool_choice" of type "any" to guarantee a tool call, but responses sometimes contain multiple parallel tool_use blocks, breaking a harness built to execute one call per turn. What change guarantees exactly one tool call per response?
answers: Add a system prompt rule instructing Claude to emit only one tool call per response.
Set "disable_parallel_tool_use" to true inside the "tool_choice" object.
Set "strict" to true on every tool definition so the API enforces one call at a time.
Force a single named tool with "tool_choice" of type "tool" instead of the "any" type.
feedbacks: Prompt instructions give only probabilistic compliance. The harness would still sometimes receive more than one tool_use block. When you need a structural guarantee, the reliable method is the API-level flag inside the "tool_choice" object.

Parallel tool use is enabled by default. So even when the "any" type forces a tool call, one response can still contain several tool_use blocks. The documented way to guarantee one tool call, and only one, when tool use is forced is to set "disable_parallel_tool_use" to true inside the "tool_choice" object.

Strict tool use guarantees that a tool's input matches its JSON schema when the tool is called. It controls the shape of the arguments in each call. It does not control whether Claude returns one tool_use block or several in a single response.

Forcing a specific named tool controls which tool is called. It does not control how many times that tool is called. Parallel tool use is still on by default with the "tool" type, so the response can still contain several tool_use blocks for the same tool.
prompt.explanation:
Forcing a tool call and limiting the number of tool calls are two separate controls in the Messages API. Setting tool_choice to the any type guarantees that Claude uses at least one of the provided tools instead of answering in text. However, parallel tool use is on by default, so one response is allowed to contain several tool_use blocks. A harness that expects one call per turn will drop or mishandle the extra calls without any warning. This is the failure described in the question.

The documented fix is to set disable_parallel_tool_use: true inside the tool_choice object. When you use this flag with the any or tool types, the guarantee changes from "at least one tool call" to "exactly one tool call." With the default auto type, the same flag means "at most one," because Claude may still answer without using any tool. It is important to set this at the API layer, because then the limit is structural: the model cannot return a second parallel call. A system prompt rule only influences behavior, and the model will sometimes ignore it.

The other approaches each solve a different problem. Switching to a forced named tool fixes which tool runs. That is useful for enforcing the order of execution, but it does not change the number of calls. Strict tool use (strict: true) guarantees that tool inputs validate against the JSON schema. It is a schema-conformance feature. It does not control the number of calls or when a tool is called. See Parallel tool use, Defining tools and tool_choice, and Strict tool use.

QUESTION: A coordinator spawns an exploration subagent that maps a legacy module's conventions, then spawns a generation subagent to produce boilerplate matching those conventions. Both are ordinary subagents (not forks) with default settings. They have no shared memory and no way to message each other. How does the generation subagent obtain the exploration findings?
answers: The generation subagent automatically inherits the coordinator's conversation history, which contains the explorer's report.
The exploration subagent delivers its findings directly to the generation subagent as soon as its own task finishes.
Both subagents read and write a shared session memory that the SDK maintains across all spawned subagents.
The coordinator includes the explorer's returned findings in the prompt it uses to spawn the generation subagent.
feedbacks: A subagent that is not a fork starts with a fresh context window. It does not receive the parent's conversation history or earlier tool results. Many people wrongly assume that subagents inherit this context automatically. This mistake leads to subagents that are missing critical information.

In this standard chain pattern, a subagent's final report goes back to the agent that spawned it. It does not go to a sibling subagent. Direct delivery from one teammate to another belongs to other collaboration modes, such as the experimental agent teams feature. Nothing in this setup is configured for that.

In this default setup, the SDK does not automatically keep a shared session memory that all subagents read and write. Each subagent runs in its own isolated conversation. With no memory configured, information goes back through the coordinator, not through a shared state layer.

In the standard chain-subagents pattern, the explorer's final report goes back to the coordinator. Each new subagent starts with an isolated context. So the coordinator must pass the relevant findings explicitly in the delegation prompt that it uses to spawn the generation subagent.
prompt.explanation:
The standard subagent pattern in the Claude Agent SDK is a hub-and-spoke topology. A coordinator spawns subagents. Each subagent runs in its own isolated context, and its final report goes back to the coordinator that spawned it. A subagent that is not a fork starts with a fresh context window. It sees its own system prompt and the prompt string that the coordinator gives it when spawning it. It does not see the parent's conversation history, earlier tool results, or another subagent's findings. In this default sequential chaining pattern, the delegation prompt is the channel for task-specific information. So the coordinator must explicitly put whatever a later subagent needs into that prompt. In this scenario, that is the explorer's report.

This design is a deliberate tradeoff. Context isolation stops long exploration output (file listings, grep results, intermediate reasoning) from filling the context of the coordinator or of other subagents. This protects the main context window and keeps each worker focused on its task. The cost is that the default configuration shares nothing automatically. The subagent does not inherit the parent's history, and there is no automatic shared memory across subagents, unless you configure such mechanisms explicitly. Expecting automatic sharing is a common cause of failures. In these failures, a later agent produces generic output because it never saw the earlier findings.

In this standard chain, results go back to the caller. Sibling subagents do not pass work to each other by themselves. Anthropic does document other collaboration modes. One example is the experimental agent teams feature, where teammates send messages to each other directly and coordinate through a shared task list. That is a separate mode from the default subagent chaining described in this question. See Subagents in the SDK and Agent teams to compare the two.

PostToolUse hooks fire only after a tool call has already completed successfully. So when the hook runs, the forbidden edit has already happened. This gives detection and auditing, not prevention. It cannot meet a requirement for guaranteed compliance.

Few-shot examples improve behavior because the model follows the pattern in them. But the agent can still behave differently in new situations. Like any prompt-based technique, examples give probabilistic compliance. They do not give the deterministic blocking that the team needs.

prompt.explanation:
This question tests the core design difference between programmatic enforcement and prompt-based guidance. In the Claude Agent SDK, a PreToolUse hook fires when the model requests a tool call, before anything runs. The hook's callback can return a permissionDecision of "deny", together with a reason that the model sees. This means the forbidden operation never runs, whatever the model intended. The hook is code that runs in your harness. It is not text that the model interprets. For this reason, it gives a deterministic guarantee: compliance no longer depends on the model's attention or judgment.

The timing of each hook event makes the choice clear. PostToolUse fires only after a tool call has succeeded. It is the right place for logging, normalizing outputs, or giving context back to the model. However, because of when it runs, it cannot prevent an action. System prompt rules, CLAUDE.md entries, and few-shot examples all work through the same channel. They shape the model's behavior and usually achieve high compliance. But the logs in this scenario show the remaining failure rate, which prompt wording cannot remove. When a rule must hold on every run, including runs with no person watching, the key idea is this: prompts ask, and hooks enforce.

Note one practical caveat. A hook's matcher defines what the hook enforces. A hook that matches only the Write and Edit tools will not catch the same file being changed through a Bash command. To protect a path reliably, you must cover every tool that can change it. Use Bash with output redirection to append the updated constant line to the end of the file.
Use Edit, passing the current constant line as "old_string" and the replacement as "new_string".

This option tries to change how a mechanism behaves by using wording. That is an anti-pattern when a tool built for partial changes already exists.

Write never merges. It overwrites the file with the content given in the call, whether or not the file was read first. Reading first may meet a permission requirement. But if Write still receives only the single line, the file still becomes that one line.

Appending to the end of the file would leave the old constant definition in the file. This creates a duplicate value that probably conflicts with the new one. It also skips the Edit tool, which was built for this purpose and replaces the text in place safely and accurately.

prompt.explanation:
The failure in this scenario happens because the tool's contract does not match what the agent intended. Write is a full-file operation. It creates a new file, or it overwrites an existing file with the content given in the call. It does not append, patch, or merge. When an agent calls Write with only the part it wants to change, the file becomes only that part. This is the data loss seen in this scenario.

The agent gives an old_string, which must appear in the file exactly as written, and a new_string to put in its place. The rest of the file is never rewritten, so a one-line change can only affect that one line. The exact-match requirement also adds safety. If the target text appears more than once, Edit refuses the unclear change. The agent must then either add surrounding context to old_string or deliberately choose to replace all occurrences. Use the PostToolUse hook to block calls that break the format rules so side effects such as file writes never occur.

This is the correct way to transform results. A PostToolUse hook can return replacement output. The model then processes only the normalized version, not the raw result. This is the documented mechanism for transforming tool results in different formats before the agent uses them.

This does not work. PostToolUse fires after the tool has already run. So any file writes, commands, or network requests have already happened when the hook runs. Preventing a call before it runs is the job of a PreToolUse hook.

This is a valid design decision. The PostToolUse hook input includes the tool name, the input parameters that were used, and the tool response. The tool has already run, and the hook runs between that execution and the moment the result enters the model's context. The hook callback receives the tool's name, the input parameters that were actually used, and the tool response. This is why a single hook can convert the results of many tools into one format. Content in the root CLAUDE.md always loads. This goes against the stated goal of keeping the conventions out of context during unrelated work. Instructions that are always loaded also compete for the model's attention with every other rule in the file.

A rule file with a paths glob, such as a glob that matches all test files, loads only when the agent works with a matching file. The matching file can be anywhere in the repository. Suppose a rule is scoped with a pattern that matches test files, for example a recursive glob over test-file extensions. That rule loads only when Claude reads, writes, or edits a matching file. CLAUDE.md gives guidance that is always loaded. But it does not change which command file Claude Code runs when the slash command is invoked. The engineer's personal command would still override the project version, so the root cause is not fixed.

Claude Code resolves name conflicts with a documented order of precedence. A personal command or skill with the same name takes precedence over the project-level one. The repository file is the same as everyone else's, and only one user sees different behavior. So the most likely cause is a user-level file that hides the shared command. When the same name exists at more than one level, Claude Code follows a documented order of precedence. Enterprise wins over personal, and personal wins over project. A skill also takes precedence over a file in .claude/commands/. In practice, this means that an old personal file on one developer's machine can override (hide) the team's shared command without any warning. Nothing in the repository will show this.

Sometimes shared, version-controlled configuration is shown to be the same on every machine (a clean git status and matching file contents), but one user still sees different behavior. QUESTION: A team configures a Claude Code PreToolUse command hook that blocks Bash commands modifying files outside the repository. An audit of unattended runs shows the hook script crashed on several occasions, and the commands it should have blocked executed anyway. What change closes this gap?

Configure the hook with "onFailure": "block" so a hook failure denies the tool call.

In this scenario, the action must be stopped before it runs. Only a check that runs before execution and fails closed can guarantee this.

Retries help only when the failure is temporary. A crash that keeps happening, such as one caused by a missing dependency or a wrong path, would still fail. The action would then still run, because crashing command hooks fail open by default. The real problem is that script failures are treated as "allow", and retries do not change that.

For Claude Code command hooks, a hook script that crashes or exits abnormally is treated as making no decision by default. So the action still runs, and a broken policy hook lets every command through without any warning. Setting "onFailure" to "block" makes the hook fail closed. This keeps the deterministic guarantee even when the enforcement script itself breaks.

Prompt instructions give only probabilistic compliance. So they cannot be the fallback protection for a rule that must hold every time. A gap in deterministic enforcement must be closed in code. It cannot be closed with guidance that the model may sometimes ignore.
prompt.explanation:
Hooks exist to turn a rule that the model usually follows into a rule that it cannot skip. A PreToolUse hook runs as code before the tool call, and it can deny the call whatever the model intended. But this guarantee is only as strong as what the hook does when it fails. For Claude Code command hooks, a hook script that crashes or fails is treated as making no decision by default, and the action runs anyway. This default is called fail-open. (This applies to Claude Code command and HTTP hooks. Agent SDK callback hooks have their own documented failure behavior, and you should not assume that they behave the same way.) For a convenience hook, such as auto-formatting, this default makes sense. For a policy hook, it means that a wrong interpreter path or a missing dependency turns off your enforcement without any warning. Setting "onFailure": "block" changes the hook to fail closed. Then, if the enforcement layer is broken, it denies the action instead of allowing it.

There are two separate reliability questions. First, does the check make the right decision when it runs? Second, what happens when the check does not run at all? Each incorrect option misses one of these questions. A system prompt rule is probabilistic by nature. That is the reason the team chose a hook. It cannot act as the fallback for a mechanism that must hold on every run. Retries cover only temporary crashes. For failures that keep happening, the fail-open default still applies, so the command runs. Moving the check to a PostToolUse hook changes when the check runs, not what it guarantees. That event fires after the tool call has completed. It can report a violation or send text back to the model, but by that time the command outside the repository has already run.

The coordinator decomposed the task too narrowly, so non-HTTP integration types were never assigned to any subagent.

The delegated subtasks cover only HTTP-style integrations. So no subagent was ever responsible for database or message queue connections. Every subagent completed its assignment correctly. So the gap started earlier, in the way the coordinator divided the broad cataloging task.

Every later stage of the system can work perfectly, and the output will still be incomplete in a consistent way. The reason is that whole categories (database connections, message queues) were never in anyone's scope.

Otherwise, subagents will repeat each other's work and leave gaps. You should diagnose coverage failures from the top down. If the subagent logs show that each subagent carried out its assignment correctly, the fault is almost always in how the work was divided, not in how it was done.

The other diagnoses put the failure in the wrong place. Grep queries that are too specific would be a real problem if a subagent had searched for database code and found nothing. But in this scenario, no subagent was assigned that search. Context isolation is an intentional feature that keeps long exploration output out of the parent conversation. It does not drop findings, and in this case there were no non-HTTP findings to drop. A coverage check on the final catalog is a useful safety net. A well-designed coordinator can use that kind of feedback to spawn more subagents in a refinement loop. But a check at the end cannot replace assigning the missing categories at the start.

QUESTION: To stop the agent answering codebase questions from memory, the team added "CRITICAL: You MUST call a tool before responding" to its system prompt. Now it runs Grep even for follow-ups already answered in the conversation. What change makes the agent call tools only when it needs to?
answers: Add a hook that blocks tool calls whenever the user's message falls below a length threshold.
Set "tool_choice" to "none" by default, switching to "auto" only when a message mentions code.
Reword the directive to normal guidance such as "use the tools to investigate when needed".
Expand each tool's description with boundary language stating when the tool should not be used.
feedbacks: Message length is a poor signal of whether investigation is needed. A short question can need a new lookup, and a long question can be answerable from the context. This option builds a custom blocking mechanism to fight behavior that the system prompt itself is causing.

Forcing "none" blocks all tool calls, including investigations that are needed. Switching based on keywords is fragile, because many codebase questions do not contain obvious trigger words. This replaces one extreme with another extreme. It does not correct the instruction that caused the overtriggering.

Very forceful words like CRITICAL and MUST push the model to call tools on every turn. This includes turns where the answer is already in context. Anthropic's guidance is to change such instructions back to plain wording. The agent then still investigates when a lookup is really needed, and it answers directly when the information is already available.

Boundary language in tool descriptions is the right fix when the agent chooses the wrong tool among tools that overlap. In this scenario, the agent chooses tools correctly. The system prompt directive is what pushes it to call a tool on every turn. So the root cause is the prompt wording, not the tool descriptions.
prompt.explanation:
The wording of the system prompt controls how readily Claude calls tools, and it can be adjusted up or down. The documentation describes a range. Wording like "use your judgment" keeps tool use low. "Use the tools to investigate before responding" increases it. "Always call a tool first" pushes it the most. Teams often add instructions with strong emphasis, such as CRITICAL or MUST, to fix undertriggering. These instructions can push behavior too far in the other direction and cause overtriggering. The model then calls a tool on every turn, even when the answer is already in context. Anthropic's prompting guidance specifically recommends replacing wording like "CRITICAL: You MUST use this tool when..." with normal wording like "Use this tool when...".

Under the default tool_choice: "auto", Claude compares the request with each tool's described capability and with what is already in context. The system prompt changes how that comparison comes out. It does not turn tool use on or off. That is why rewording the directive is the right fix in this scenario, and why the other approaches fail. Adding boundaries to tool descriptions decides which tool is selected when descriptions overlap. It does not decide whether a tool is called at all. Forcing tool_choice to "none" and turning tools back on by keyword blocks needed investigation behind a fragile, simple rule. A message-length hook blocks tool calls based on a signal that has nothing to do with whether investigation is actually needed. If you ever need a guaranteed tool call, the documented mechanism is tool_choice, not stronger prompt wording. In the same way, when the problem is too many tool calls, the fix is softer prompt wording, not new enforcement mechanisms.

See Tool use overview and Claude prompting best practices.

QUESTION: The agent must find every call site of a utility function "formatCurrency" that several wrapper modules re-export under different alias names. Which TWO steps form the correct tracing workflow? (Select TWO.)
answers: Glob for each alias across file contents, since identifiers can be expressed as path patterns.
Grep the codebase for each exported alias to locate call sites that import through the wrappers.
Grep only for "formatCurrency", since every call path resolves to the original function name.
Read each wrapper module to identify every name under which "formatCurrency" is exported.
feedbacks: Glob matches file names and paths against patterns. It does not search inside files. Finding where an identifier is used is a content search, and content search is Grep's job. So this choice mixes up the jobs of the two tools.

Grep searches file contents, and that is what you need to find where an identifier is used. Searching for every alias, not only the original name, finds the callers that reach the function indirectly through a wrapper module.

Code that imports the function through a wrapper uses the alias, not the original name. So a search for the original name alone misses those call sites. The workflow that finds the exported names first exists to close this gap.

Wrapper modules can rename a function when they re-export it. So the only way to find the exported alias names is to inspect the wrappers themselves. Reading those files first gives the complete list of names to search for. You need this list before you can find every call site.
prompt.explanation:
Tracing usage through wrapper modules is a problem with two stages. A wrapper can re-export a function under a different name. This means the identifier at the call site is the alias, not the original name. So if you search for the original name alone, the results look complete but are not. The search succeeds and returns results, but it leaves out every caller that imports through a wrapper, and nothing tells you that they are missing. The reliable workflow is to list the names first and then search for each of them. First, use Read (or a targeted Grep for export statements) on the wrapper files to collect every exported alias. Only then run Grep across the codebase for each name on that list.

This follows the same staged exploration that Anthropic documents for work on a codebase. First find the relevant files, then understand how they relate to each other, then trace the flow. No tool has a built-in mode that finds exports before searching. It is a workflow that the agent must be told to follow. For this reason, it is useful to write it explicitly in prompts or agent instructions when completeness matters.

It also matters which search tool does which job. Glob matches file paths against name patterns and never looks inside files. So it cannot find where an identifier is used. That is the job of Grep, which performs regex search over file contents. Treating an alias as something Glob could match uses a path-matching tool for a content-search task. Searching only for the original function name is a less obvious failure. It is the first thing most people would try. It works perfectly in codebases that have no re-export layers. That is why people keep doing it, until a wrapper module hides half of the call sites.

See the Claude Code tools reference for how Grep and Glob behave, and Common workflows for the documented exploration pattern of finding files first and then tracing the flow.

QUESTION: An agent running an automated migration fails partway through. The agent used subagents to investigate parts of the failure, and it must now escalate to an on-call engineer who has no access to the session transcript or the subagents' sessions. Which two practices produce an effective handoff? (Select TWO.)
answers: Compile a self-contained summary with the task identifiers, the root cause analysis so far, and a recommended next action.
Attach every raw tool output the agent collected so the engineer can inspect all underlying evidence directly.
Include subagent findings and evidence directly in the handoff instead of referencing those subagents' isolated sessions.
Send only the task identifier and failure category so the engineer forms an independent diagnosis without being influenced by the agent's analysis.
feedbacks: The engineer who receives the handoff cannot see the transcript. So the handoff itself must contain the complete state of the case. A structured summary with identifiers, the analysis done so far, and a recommended action lets the engineer continue the work. The engineer does not have to restart the investigation.

Sending raw tool outputs passes on noise, not the state of the case. It forces the engineer to repeat the analysis that the agent already did. A selected summary of findings is much more useful than a large amount of raw evidence with no interpretation.

Subagents run in isolated contexts, and only their final results go back to the parent. No one after them can see their intermediate work. The investigation was delegated to subagents. So their conclusions and supporting evidence must be written into the handoff itself.

Holding back the completed investigation so that the engineer can look with fresh eyes throws away work the agent already did. It forces the engineer to start from zero. The agent's root cause analysis and recommendation are what make a handoff valuable. The engineer can still disagree with them.
prompt.explanation:
No transcript goes with an escalation unless your application sends one. The Messages API is stateless. Your code must explicitly collect and pass every piece of context that Claude or a person sees, as described in Working with Messages. When the engineer who receives the case has no access to the session, the agent must produce a self-contained handoff artifact. It contains task identifiers, the root cause analysis done so far, relevant evidence, and a recommended next action. This lets the engineer continue the case from where it stopped, instead of running the whole investigation again.

The same logic applies to subagents. A subagent runs in its own isolated context, and only its final message goes back to the parent. Its intermediate exploration cannot be seen afterward. A handoff that says "see the subagent's work" points to something that no one can read. So the subagent's conclusions and evidence must be included in the summary directly. Many teams enforce this shape with Structured Outputs. They define a JSON schema with required fields (identifiers, root cause, recommended action), and this helps produce and validate handoff JSON that can be parsed. This helps, but it is not a guarantee in every case. A response with a stop_reason of refusal or max_tokens may not match the schema. So a reliable flow checks the stop reason and the validation results before it puts the handoff in the human queue. See Structured Outputs.

The incorrect options fail in opposite directions. Forwarding every raw tool output passes on volume, not understanding. The context windows documentation notes that accuracy and recall get worse as inputs grow, and a human reviewer has the same problem. Selected findings are better than a large amount of raw output with no interpretation. Sending only an identifier and a category goes too far in the other direction. It throws away the completed analysis, so the person who receives the escalation (the engineer) must find everything again. This defeats the purpose of escalating a case that was already partly investigated.

QUESTION: A teammate proposes that the codebase-exploration subagent should hand its findings straight to the boilerplate-generation subagent, skipping the coordinator to reduce round trips. Which design preserves observability and controlled information flow?
answers: Grant both subagents a peer-messaging tool so the explorer can send its findings directly to the generator.
Have each subagent report back to the coordinator, which includes the relevant findings in the next subagent's prompt.
Have both subagents write to and read from a shared scratchpad file to exchange intermediate results.
Give the generator subagent the same repository tools and have it re-run the exploration itself before generating.
feedbacks: Subagents can technically send messages to each other. But this moves communication outside the coordinator's view. It weakens observability and consistent error handling. Use it only when direct communication between peers is an intentional design goal, not as a shortcut to avoid the coordinator.

This is the hub-and-spoke pattern. The coordinator sees every result, applies consistent error handling, and decides what context each subagent receives. An ordinary non-fork subagent starts without the parent's conversation or the results of another agent. So the coordinator passing the findings forward in the prompt is the intended communication channel.

A shared file creates a side channel that no one tracks. The coordinator cannot see what was exchanged or validate it. It also cannot handle failures when one subagent writes incomplete or out-of-date data. A scratchpad helps one agent keep its findings during its own work. It does not replace coordinated handoffs between agents.

Exploring again repeats the explorer's work, which roughly doubles the tokens and the latency. The generator may also find different things than the explorer did. It also avoids the handoff completely, so the coordinator never selects or validates the information that the generator acts on.
prompt.explanation:
In a coordinator-subagent (hub-and-spoke) architecture, all communication between agents goes through the coordinator by design. An ordinary non-fork subagent receives task-specific content from the parent through the prompt that the coordinator writes for it. Only its final report goes back to the parent. Fork subagents are a documented exception: they can inherit the parent conversation. But even a fork does not inherit the context of a sibling subagent. This isolation is what makes the pattern work. It keeps long exploration output out of other agents' contexts. It also makes the coordinator the single place where results are observed, where errors are handled in a consistent way, and where information is deliberately selected before it is passed on. When the explorer finishes, the coordinator reads its report and includes the relevant findings in the generator subagent's prompt.

The tempting alternative is to give subagents a tool for sending messages to each other. This tool does exist in the Claude Agent SDK. But it gives up what the question asks you to keep. Once agents send messages to each other directly, the coordinator no longer sees every exchange. It cannot apply consistent error handling, and it loses control over what information each worker receives. A shared scratchpad file has the same problem in a different form. Data is exchanged through a side channel that the coordinator never inspects. Having the generator explore the repository again avoids a handoff instead of designing one. It repeats the explorer's work at a real cost in tokens and latency. It may find different things. It still leaves the coordinator with no control over what information the generator acts on.

Subagents are isolated workers, and the coordinator is the router. For non-fork subagents, the prompt written by the coordinator and the final report are the approved channels between them. Routing through the coordinator takes slightly more steps. In return, you get observability, because every delegation and result is visible, and tracing tools can even show subagent activity nested under the coordinator's calls. You also get consistent recovery when a worker fails, and exact control over context. See Subagents in the SDK and Agent SDK Observability for the documented behavior.

QUESTION: A research subagent's "fetch_report" MCP tool reports failures with "isError": true plus two custom fields the team added, "errorCategory" and "isRetryable". When the archive denies access to a source outside the team's subscription, the tool returns "errorCategory": "transient" with "isRetryable": true, so the subagent keeps retrying the same call until it runs out of attempts. Which change fixes the recovery behavior?
answers: Return the denial as a permission error with "isRetryable": false so the subagent escalates instead of retrying.
Add exponential backoff between successive retry attempts so the repeated calls place less load on the archive service.
Have the tool catch the denial and return an empty result marked as successful so no retries are triggered.
Add a system prompt rule telling the subagent to stop retrying any tool call that fails twice in a row.
feedbacks: An access denial is a permission error, not a transient failure. Retrying cannot succeed, because the subscription does not cover the source. The correct category with a non-retryable flag tells the agent, at the moment it decides, to stop retrying. The agent can then escalate or continue without that source.

Backoff is the right treatment for transient errors such as timeouts or temporary overload. But this failure is deterministic. Waiting does not change what the subscription covers, so every retry still fails. The wrong category is still the root cause.

Marking a failure as a success hides the error without any warning, which is a known anti-pattern. The agent and the coordinator would treat the missing source as a valid empty result. The coverage gap would be hidden from the final report, instead of being shown so that someone can make an informed decision.

A general prompt rule is probabilistic. It is also wrong for real transient failures, which may correctly need more than two attempts. The reliable mechanism is the error metadata itself. It gives the agent the retry decision on the first failure.
prompt.explanation:
Structured error metadata exists so that an agent can make the right recovery decision at the moment a tool call fails. In MCP and in Claude tool use, the documented mechanism is the error flag itself. Tool execution failures that the model can act on are returned in a normal tool result with isError: true (or is_error in a Claude tool result). This lets the model see the failure and correct itself. Fields like errorCategory and isRetryable are not part of that specification. They are metadata that a team defines and adds to the error content. In this system's convention, each category maps to a different behavior. Transient errors (timeouts, temporary unavailability) should be retried, often with backoff. Validation errors should make the agent fix its input and try again. Business errors (policy violations) should be explained, not retried. Permission errors (access denied) should be escalated. The isRetryable flag states the retry decision explicitly, so the agent does not have to guess it.

An access denial based on the subscription is deterministic. The request was well formed and the service was working, but the caller is not authorized to use that resource. Labeling it transient misleads the agent. The metadata says that retrying might work, but it never can. Changing the response to a permission error with "isRetryable": false fixes the behavior at its source. The agent stops after the first failure and can escalate or note the gap in its findings. This matches how the MCP specification describes tool failures. Execution errors are returned in the tool result with isError: true so that the model can recover in a sensible way. They should not be hidden or given the wrong label.

The other approaches each miss the point. Exponential backoff treats the problem as if it were a temporary outage. A prompt rule to stop calling after two failures is a rough, general rule. It does not give real transient errors enough attempts, and it depends on probabilistic compliance. Returning an empty result marked as successful hides the error completely. A known access limit then becomes false information in the final report, and no one can tell it is false. See the MCP tools specification on execution errors and handling tool calls for how error results are returned to the model.

QUESTION: A multi-agent research system defines each subagent programmatically with an AgentDefinition, and every subagent currently inherits the full tool catalog. Logs show the report-writing subagent updating issue-tracker records and the document-analysis subagent running broad web research. Which change restricts each subagent to only the tools its role needs?
answers: Set each subagent's "tools" field in its AgentDefinition to its role-relevant tools, leaving unrelated tools out of its session.
Add a rule to each subagent's system prompt naming the tools outside its role that it must never call.
List each role's tool names in the session-level "allowedTools" setting so those tools are pre-approved for the subagents.
Rewrite every tool description to state which subagent role it belongs to, keeping the full catalog available.
feedbacks: When a subagent's AgentDefinition lists specific tools, the subagent receives only those tools. Any tool that is not on the list is not present in its session at all. There is no permission prompt and no error. This is the documented mechanism for limiting each role to a small set of relevant tools. It is the design-level fix for subagents using tools that belong to other roles.

Prompt instructions are probabilistic guidance, not enforcement. A subagent that still has the full catalog in its session can still call tools outside its role, and sometimes it will, despite the instruction. This is the failure that already appears in the logs.

The "allowedTools" setting pre-approves the listed tools so that they run without permission prompts. But tools that are not on the list are still available. It changes approval behavior, not availability. So a subagent could still select and call tools outside its role.

Tool descriptions help a model choose correctly among the tools it has. But they do not remove any tool. The full catalog is still present in every subagent's session. So tool selection is still less reliable, and calls to tools outside the role are still possible.
prompt.explanation:
The reliable way to keep a subagent within its role is to control which tools exist in its session. Asking it to ignore tools it can see is not reliable. In the Claude Agent SDK, each subagent's AgentDefinition has an optional tools field. If the field is omitted, the subagent inherits every tool that is available to subagents. If the field lists tools, the subagent gets only those tools. A tool that is not on the list is not blocked or placed behind a permission prompt. It does not exist for that subagent at all, so Claude plans and works without it. This matters for two reasons. First, agents choose much more reliably from a small number of tools relevant to their role than from a large catalog. So limiting the tools makes selection more accurate for the tools that remain. Second, using tools outside the role becomes structurally impossible, not only discouraged.

The tempting alternative, allowedTools, solves a different problem. It pre-approves the listed tools so that they run without interactive permission checks. But Anthropic's documentation clearly states that tools outside the list are still available. The active permission mode only controls what happens when a tool that is not on the list is called. It is a convenience and permission mechanism, not a way to limit which tools exist. System prompt rules and better tool descriptions are both valid techniques. But they work probabilistically on a subagent that still has the full catalog. Descriptions improve selection among the available tools. Prompt rules depend on compliance, and the production logs already show that compliance is not perfect. When the goal is that a report-writing agent cannot change the issue tracker at all, the tool must be removed at the definition level.

See Agent SDK Subagents for how the tools field behaves and for patterns that restrict tools by role, and Agent SDK Configuration for why allowedTools pre-approves tools instead of restricting them.

QUESTION: The synthesis agent receives roughly 80K tokens of aggregated subagent findings in a single prompt. Evaluation shows it reliably uses material from the opening and closing sections but regularly overlooks relevant findings in the middle. How should you restructure this input?
answers: Compress every subagent's output into a short summary so the combined input stays under 20K tokens.
Place a key-findings summary at the top of the input and label detailed sections with explicit headings.
Rotate which subagent's findings appear first on each run so every source gets top placement over time.
Add a system prompt instruction directing the synthesis agent to weigh all sections of the input equally.
feedbacks: Heavy summarization of all findings removes exact details, such as figures, dates, and source attributions, that the synthesis step needs. The position problem can be solved with structure. You do not have to lose the detail that makes the research report useful.

Models pay attention most reliably to the beginning and the end of long inputs. So moving critical findings to the top puts them in a position that gets strong attention. Explicit section headings give the model clear structural markers. These make content in the middle of the input easier to find and use.

Rotation only changes which content is missed on each run. It does not stop content from being missed. Every single report still has weak attention to whatever ends up in the middle, so the quality of synthesis stays inconsistent.

The lost-in-the-middle effect comes from how the model processes long inputs. It is not a failure to follow instructions. Telling the model to pay equal attention does not bring back the attention. Changing where critical content is placed does.
prompt.explanation:
This scenario shows the lost-in-the-middle effect. When an input is tens of thousands of tokens long, models process the beginning and the end most reliably, and content in the middle gets weaker attention. Anthropic's own long-context research placed answer passages at the beginning, middle, and end of long inputs, and found that recall changed with position. This has a practical result for a multi-agent system. Suppose an aggregation step only joins subagent outputs together. It will consistently give too little weight to whichever findings end up in the middle of the input, even when those findings directly answer the research question.

The structural fix is ordering the input with position in mind. Put a short key-findings summary at the very top of the aggregated input, where attention is strongest. Then organize the detailed results below it with explicit section headings (XML tags or clear headers). These give the model clear markers that help it find content in the middle of the document. This matches Anthropic's guidance to deliberately structure long prompts that contain a lot of data, instead of treating them as one block with no structure. Note that this works together with keeping the input small. It does not replace that. The Context windows documentation warns that accuracy can get worse as the number of tokens grows. So selecting content and structuring it work together.

Each incorrect approach misses the mechanism. Compressing everything into a very short summary removes the position problem but creates a new problem: the summary loses information. It removes the figures and attributions that a report with citations depends on. Rotating the order of sections only changes which findings get dropped on each run. A prompt instruction to pay equal attention asks the model to override a processing characteristic that instructions alone do not change. See Claude prompting best practices and Prompting long context for the guidance on structuring long inputs.

QUESTION: A client requests research that requires pulling content from a login-protected third-party website. The team's source-usage policy covers public web sources and the licensed internal repository, but does not mention login-protected websites. What should the coordinator do?
answers: Have the coordinator rate its confidence that access is allowed and proceed when confidence is high.
Proceed by applying the licensed-repository rules to the website, since the cases are very similar.
Escalate the request to a human operator, flagging that the source-usage policy does not address it.
Decline the request, informing the client that accessing login-protected third-party websites is against policy.
feedbacks: The model's rating of its own confidence is not a reliable signal of whether an action is actually allowed. The model can be confident and wrong, especially on cases that the policy never expected. Gaps in policy need human judgment, not a threshold on the agent's own uncertainty.

Extending a related rule by analogy means that the agent invents policy coverage that was never given. The licensed repository is covered by an explicit agreement. A login-protected third-party website may have completely different terms. So reasoning by analogy can commit the organization to actions that it is not authorized to take.

When the policy says nothing about the specific request, the agent should report the gap to a person instead of inventing a rule. An authorized person can then decide whether access is acceptable. This keeps the agent within the policy it was actually given, and it does not guess beyond that policy.

Declining for this reason claims a prohibition that the policy never states. This is still inventing policy, only in the restrictive direction. The policy says nothing about the case; it does not forbid it. So the honest action is to report the gap for a person to resolve, not to claim that a rule exists.
prompt.explanation:
The basic principle is that an agent's authority comes only from the policy it was given. Where the policy says nothing, the agent has no authority to act and no authority to refuse. In this scenario, the rules cover a related situation (the licensed internal repository) but not the current one (a login-protected third-party website). Escalating in this case matches Anthropic's guidance for support-style agents. The agent should recognize when a query needs human intervention. It should give only information that is based on the stated coverage. It should not guess beyond that coverage or make commitments that the system is not authorized to make. The correct behavior is to escalate with a clear statement of the gap, so that a person with real authority can decide.

The two options where the agent makes its own decision fail in opposite ways. Extending the repository rules by analogy in effect invents a permission. This can make commitments that the organization never authorized. The API does not require any execution order for parallel tool calls. The application may run them at the same time or one after another, as it chooses. What matters is that one result is returned for each call. The order in which the tools ran does not matter.

Every tool_use block has a unique id. The matching tool_result must refer to that id in its tool_use_id field. This pairing is how the API connects each result to the specific call that requested it. This is especially important when several tools run in one turn.

A single assistant turn can contain several tool_use blocks, because parallel tool use is the default. So the protocol needs a clear way to pair every request with its result. That pairing is the id on each tool_use block. The harness copies it back as tool_use_id on the matching tool_result block. The message structure is just as strict. All of the tool_result blocks go in one user message. This message must come immediately after the assistant message that contains the calls, and the results must come before any text in that message.

A tool that fails still gets a tool_result, with is_error set to true and the error message as content. Claude can then reason about the failure and change its next action. Leaving out the result, or describing the error in free text, breaks the pairing between calls and results. This makes it harder for the model to recover from the failure.

Next, have Claude review that draft against specific criteria (every claim is cited, the template is followed). Then have Claude refine the draft based on the review. Each stage is a separate call, and this is what makes the pattern valuable in production. The application can inspect, log, or evaluate the intermediate outputs, or take different actions based on them. Instruct the agent in the same session to ignore the first version before producing the second.
Resume the session by its ID for each version, since resuming restores the evaluation context.
Start two fresh sessions and paste a condensed summary of the source evaluation into each one.
feedbacks: Forking a session creates a new session that starts with a copy of the original history. The original session does not change. Resume the analysis session twice with the fork flag set. Each version then gets the full source evaluation as a shared starting point. After that, each branch develops under its own session ID and cannot see the other branch.

An instruction cannot make the model forget part of the conversation context. The first version stays in the history and can influence the second version. This uses a prompt to try to get a guarantee that only session branching actually gives.

Resuming without the fork flag continues the one original session. It does not create a branch. The second version would resume a history that already contains the output of the first version. This would make the comparison that the team wants to make unfair.

A condensed summary is only an approximation of the completed evaluation, and it loses information. It also has to be prepared and inserted twice. Forking copies the complete analysis history into both branches. You do not pay for the analysis again, and you do not risk losing details.
prompt.explanation:
Forking is the session-management mechanism built for this situation: exploring in different directions from a shared starting point. A fork creates a new session that starts with a copy of the original history. The original session does not change, and you can still resume it separately. In the Agent SDK, you trigger a fork at query time by resuming an existing session with the fork flag set. For example, use ClaudeAgentOptions(resume=session_id, fork_session=True) in Python or { resume: sessionId, forkSession: true } in TypeScript. Each fork gets its own session ID. So the two report versions both inherit the full evaluation of the 30 sources, but after that they develop separately, and neither one affects the other.

The other options fail because of what a session is. A session is saved conversation history: prompts, tool calls, tool results, and responses written to disk. Resuming by ID without forking adds to that one shared history. So a second version would see the output of the first version. Pasting a summary into fresh sessions replaces the full evaluation with an approximation that loses information and must be maintained by hand. Asking the model to ignore earlier content is a probabilistic instruction, and the content is still present in the context. Branching, in contrast, guarantees separation by design.

Note one limit. Forking branches the conversation, not the filesystem. If both forked branches edit files in the same working directory, each session can see the other's edits. To keep files separate, you need checkpointing or worktrees. See Agent SDK Sessions and the Python Agent SDK reference for the fork options and their limits.

Fitting more content into the context does not fix inconsistent attention. Performance gets worse as the window fills, whatever its size. The problem is the single-pass structure, not whether the files fit.

A subagent for each file gives each file a focused, isolated context. So the depth of analysis stays consistent, instead of being divided across 16 files. Each subagent returns only a summary, so the long file contents stay out of the coordinator's context.

Per-file passes cannot see how files interact. So a separate integration pass is needed for cross-file issues, such as mismatched types, circular dependencies, and the same pattern being treated in different ways. Reviewing all the per-file summaries in one place also resolves the contradictory feedback.

In this scenario, some files get deep comments, others get shallow comments, and identical code gets opposite verdicts. This failure pattern is attention dilution. When one pass must cover many files, the model cannot keep the same depth of analysis for all of them. The documented fix is a change in structure, not a bigger context window. Claude Code's guidance clearly states that performance gets worse as the context window fills. So the goal is to keep each unit of analysis small and focused, not to fit more into a single pass.

The local-then-global pattern does this. Each file gets its own self-contained pass. In the Agent SDK, the natural building block for this is a subagent. A subagent runs in its own context window. It does the long, detailed exploration and analysis there, and it returns only a findings summary to the parent. These per-file investigations are independent, so the coordinator can spawn them in parallel. A separate integration pass then works on the collected summaries. It examines what no per-file pass can see: data flow between files, type consistency, and whether the same pattern is treated the same way everywhere. Non-fork subagents do not share state with each other. So this cross-file phase belongs at the point where all the summaries come together, in the coordinator or in a synthesis step.

The incorrect options both diagnose the problem wrongly. A larger context window deals with capacity, not with the quality of attention. The files may already fit, and the depth still varies. Majority voting across repeated single-pass runs makes the flaw worse. Detection is inconsistent, so real bugs found in only one run are thrown away, and the structural cause is never fixed.

User-scoped configuration in ~/.claude.json does keep keys out of the repository. But it gives up the goal of shared team configuration. Every developer would have to create and maintain the server definition by hand, and the configurations would become different over time.

Environment variable expansion in .mcp.json is the documented pattern for this problem. The committed file contains only the reference ${SEARCH_API_KEY}. Claude Code expands it at runtime from each developer's local environment. So the team shares the server configuration, and the secret never enters the repository.

Committing a secret in plain text to version control is an anti-pattern, whatever the repository permissions are. The key stays in the git history. Anyone who ever gets read access can see it. It cannot be rotated without changing the configuration for the whole team.
prompt.explanation:
Claude Code supports environment variable expansion in .mcp.json. Its purpose is to let teams commit shared MCP server configuration while keeping secrets and machine-specific values out of the repository. The syntax is ${VAR}, with an optional fallback form ${VAR:-default}. Expansion works in the command, args, env, url, and headers fields of a server definition. Each developer sets the variable in their own shell or settings, and Claude Code resolves it at runtime.

The secrets those servers need are specific to each machine, and they belong in the local environment. Moving the server into ~/.claude.json keeps the secret private but stops the configuration from being shared. Every developer must then copy and maintain the definition by hand. Glob searches only the outside of files in the file system: names, extensions, and directory paths. A request like "which files contain X" is a Grep task. A request like "which files have a name or location like X" is a Glob task.

Grep also suits this checking task well because it can report results at different levels of detail. Its default mode returns only the paths of files that contain a match. That is the output the agent needs to "identify every file that mentions this phrase." Patterns use ripgrep regex syntax, not POSIX grep syntax. So literal punctuation, such as the period in "et al.", may need escaping. Results can also be limited to certain file types or glob patterns when the corpus contains different kinds of files.

The tool list in the scenario matters. On macOS, Linux, and WSL, Grep and Glob are not in the default tool set, and Claude searches through Bash with find and grep instead. When Grep is enabled, the shell route through Bash is no longer the documented method for content search. The Grep tool, built for this purpose, returns results that the agent can act on directly. QUESTION: The team is adding an MCP server whose tools query a hand-picked, pre-indexed collection of research documents; subagents also keep built-in Read and Grep for local files. What should each MCP tool description emphasize so subagents select these tools when appropriate?
answers: Keep each description to a single sentence so the tool catalog consumes minimal context.
Give each tool a distinctive name, since the model selects tools primarily by their names.
State what each tool returns and the unique indexed data that built-in file tools cannot provide.
Add a coordinator prompt rule telling every subagent to always prefer MCP tools over built-in tools.
feedbacks: Very short descriptions are a documented anti-pattern that makes tool selection unreliable. Anthropic recommends at least three to four sentences that cover what the tool does, when to use it, and what it returns. The small token cost gives much more reliable routing.

Names help the model tell tools apart, but they are not the main selection signal. The model chooses tools mainly from their descriptions. A tool with a distinctive name and a short, vague description will still be skipped in favor of familiar built-in tools, whose behavior the model already understands well.

Tool descriptions are the main mechanism that the model uses when it selects a tool. Agents may choose familiar built-in tools by default when the advantages of an MCP tool are not stated clearly. Describing the tool's outputs, and the unique data or context that Read and Grep cannot provide, gives the model a clear reason to choose the MCP tool.

Prompt instructions are probabilistic guidance. A general rule to always prefer MCP tools would cause wrong tool use when a built-in tool is actually the right choice, such as when reading a local file. Anthropic also warns against this kind of over-prompting. Tool selection should be based on clear descriptions, not on one rule for every case.
prompt.explanation:
When an agent has both built-in tools and MCP tools that can do similar work, it tends to choose the built-in tools it knows well, Read and Grep. It does this unless the tool description tells it why the MCP tool is better for the job. Anthropic says that detailed descriptions are by far the most important factor in tool performance. When the model selects a tool, the description is what it actually reads. So the description should say what the tool does, when to use it (and when not to), and, most importantly, what it returns. For an MCP tool that uses a hand-picked, pre-indexed collection, this means naming the specific advantage. An example is results ranked by relevance over a pre-indexed corpus, with metadata that grep-style text matching over raw files can never produce. When the description points out unique data and outputs, the model no longer chooses at random between capabilities that seem similar. It makes an informed routing decision.

Tool selection depends on the information available when the model decides, not on general policies. A coordinator prompt that says "always prefer MCP tools" applies one rule to every situation. This makes the model use the MCP tools too often, including when reading a local file is correct. The documentation explicitly warns against this kind of general prompting. Shortening descriptions to one sentence to save context saves a few tokens but makes routing consistently worse. The guidance is at least three to four sentences per tool, and more for complex tools. Clear names help, but the model selects mainly by description. So a well-named tool with a short, vague description still loses to familiar built-in tools.

See Define tools for description best practices and Claude Code MCP for how MCP tool definitions are shown to the agent.

SCENARIO: You are building a multi-agent research system using the Claude Agent SDK. A coordinator agent delegates to specialized subagents: one searches the web, one analyzes documents, one synthesizes findings, and one generates reports. The system researches topics and produces comprehensive, cited reports.

QUESTION: You are deciding whether the coordinator should dynamically choose which subagents to spawn or follow a hard-coded invocation sequence (search, analyze, synthesize, report). Which two design recommendations are correct? (Select TWO.)
answers: Build a separate routing classifier, since the coordinator cannot select subagents on its own.
Let the coordinator choose which subagents to spawn dynamically when intermediate findings determine the next step.
Use a fixed invocation sequence when every research task follows the same stages and reproducibility matters.
Rely on model-driven delegation alone for mandatory steps, since the coordinator always invokes every required subagent.
feedbacks: This is not a valid recommendation. Claude delegates to subagents based on the task and on each subagent's description. The coordinator does not need an external routing classifier to decide which subagent to invoke. Model-driven selection is the default behavior. It does not need extra infrastructure.

This is a valid recommendation. In an agentic design, Claude decides on each turn which tool or subagent to invoke next, based on the current context and earlier results. For example, the coordinator can skip document analysis when a search returns nothing. It can also spawn more searches when the findings show new directions to explore. This ability to adapt is the main advantage of model-driven decisions for open-ended research.

This is a valid recommendation. Anthropic separates workflows from agents. Workflows coordinate LLMs and tools through predefined code paths. Agents direct their own process. Workflows are recommended when the task is well defined and consistency matters. When every research task really follows the same stages, a fixed sequence gives up some flexibility to gain reliability.

This is not a valid recommendation. Model-driven decisions are probabilistic. The coordinator may sometimes skip a step that the prompt instructions describe as required. When a step must never be skipped, the guarantee must come from deterministic mechanisms, not from the model's own reasoning. Examples are explicit invocation, deterministic orchestration in code, or programmatic validation before the result is finalized.
prompt.explanation:
This question tests the core design difference that Anthropic describes in Building Effective Agents. A workflow coordinates the model and its tools through predefined code paths. An agent lets the model dynamically direct its own process and tool use. Neither one is always better. They are at opposite ends of a range: more predictable or more flexible. A hard-coded pipeline is reproducible and easy to debug. That makes it the right choice when every task really follows the same stages. A model-driven coordinator is the better choice when the right next step depends on what was just found. This is typical of open-ended research. For example, a search that returns few results might justify spawning more search subagents. A large set of documents might justify going directly to analysis.

In the Agent SDK loop, the application defines what is available (the subagents and tools). Claude chooses among them on each turn, based on context and earlier results. That is why the coordinator does not need a separate routing classifier. Subagent selection is based on the task and on each subagent's description. The recommendation to build a classifier misunderstands how delegation works, and building one would add infrastructure that is not needed.

The other side of this flexibility is that model-driven choices are probabilistic, not guaranteed. Suppose a step is mandatory, for example a citation-verification pass before the report is finalized. If you rely on the coordinator's judgment, there is still a failure rate above zero. The deterministic options are to orchestrate that step in code, to invoke the required subagent explicitly, or to add programmatic validation that blocks completion until the step has run. Hooks such as PreToolUse can validate or block a tool call that the model has already requested. But they cannot force the model to make a call that it skipped. So for steps that must run, hooks add to deterministic orchestration but do not replace it.

QUESTION: Different MCP tools in this system return dates as Unix timestamps, ISO 8601 strings, and plain text, and subagents sometimes misread them. Which two implementation choices correctly normalize these results before the model processes them? (Select TWO.)
answers: Register a "PostToolUse" hook that returns "updatedToolOutput" with all dates converted to one standard format.
Describe each tool's date conventions in every subagent's system prompt so the model converts values itself.
Scope the hook with a matcher on the tools' full names in the "mcp__SERVER__TOOL" naming pattern.
Register a "PreToolUse" hook that rewrites the returned dates by setting "updatedInput" on each call.
feedbacks: PostToolUse fires when a tool returns a result. This is the documented point in the lifecycle for transforming outputs before Claude sees them. Returning updatedToolOutput replaces the tool result with the normalized version. This gives a deterministic guarantee that every date reaches the model in the same format.

Prompt instructions give only probabilistic compliance. The model may still misread a Unix timestamp or an unclear date on some of the calls. When consistent formats are required, deterministic transformation in a hook is the right mechanism. You should not rely on the model to convert the data.

MCP tools appear in tool lifecycle hook events under names like mcp__research__search, and hook matchers filter by tool name. A matcher on these full names, or a pattern that covers them, makes the normalizer fire only on the MCP tools that return dates in different formats.

PreToolUse runs before the tool runs. Its updatedInput field changes the arguments sent to the tool, not the data the tool returns. At that point the tool result does not exist yet. So a PreToolUse hook cannot normalize output formats.
prompt.explanation:
In the Claude Agent SDK, hooks are code that runs at fixed points in the agent lifecycle. Each event happens on a specific side of tool execution: before it or after it. PreToolUse fires before a tool runs, and it can change the arguments with updatedInput. PostToolUse fires after the tool returns, and it can replace what the model sees with updatedToolOutput. Normalizing results in different formats (Unix timestamps, ISO 8601 strings, free-text dates) is by definition a transformation of the result. So it belongs in PostToolUse. The replacement happens before Claude processes the output. This means the model only ever reasons over the standard format. It also happens in deterministic code, so it works on every call, not only on most calls.

The second part of the design is choosing which tools the hook applies to. Tool lifecycle hooks match on the tool name. MCP tools appear under full names that follow the mcp__SERVER__TOOL convention (for example mcp__memory__create_entities). A matcher on those names, or a pattern such as mcp__.* that matches every name beginning with mcp__, limits the normalizer to the tools that produce inconsistent formats. It does not affect built-in tools such as Read or Grep, whose replacement output would also have to match their schemas.

The incorrect choices show two classic failures. Rewriting dates with updatedInput in PreToolUse mixes up the two sides of execution. At that point there is no result to rewrite, only arguments that are about to be sent. Describing the formats in subagent system prompts is the usual mistake of relying on prompt guidance. It can reduce the error rate, but it cannot guarantee correct interpretation. Data normalization is a mechanical rule of the kind that should be enforced in code, not requested from the model.

See the Agent SDK hooks guide for PostToolUse output replacement, the hooks reference for event behavior and MCP tool matching, and the Agent SDK MCP guide for the tool naming convention.
